Mr. Chairman, this debate on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, although in this case restricted in time, does afford to the parties in the house-if not unfortunately to very many individual members-the opportunity to state their views in respect of at least some of the great international issues which face the world. As the available time is limited, it is necessary to concentrate on the highlights. Before I go into this in detail, however, I should like to consider in a very general way the sort of world in which we live. Barbara Ward, in a book entitled, "Spaceship Earth" has summed it up well in the following phrase:
In our world today all the irresistible forces of technology and scientific change are creating a single, vulnerable, human community."
The primary task of this generation is to create functioning world wide institutions. These institutions are required to breach the
[Mr. Diefenbaker.i
gaps of power, of wealth and of ideology which threaten the world with unprecedented disaster in the nuclear age.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I propose to discuss two of the continuing problems which face the world today. I also wish to address myself to one immediate issue; failure to solve this immediate problem will make progress in the solution of other problems difficult if not impossible. The continuing problems to which I refer are, first, the need for reconciliation between one quarter of the world which is governed by the People's Republic of China and the rest of the world. The second is the question of the vast and growing disparity between the extreme poverty of one part of the world and the relative affluence of the other part. The immediate problem to which I refer, and to which the right hon, Leader of the Opposition already has referred, is the continuation of the war in Viet Nam which stands as an obstacle to progress toward a more orderly world community. During the past week the government of Canada, at long last after many years of wavering, has taken a step forward in openly proclaiming in the United Nations the vital importance to that organization of securing the adherence of the People's Republic of China and, indeed, has made proposals designed to bring this about. I will have more to say about the Canadian proposal later.
In so far as this represents an important step in the direction which we in this party have urged for many years, we naturally welcome it and commend the government for its initiative. Later, I propose to suggest that the government go further if its initiative is to bear fruit and, indeed, if its initiative is not to appear hypocritical and unreal.

Before doing so, I should like to ask the committee to take a look at the broad general situation. Since 1949 the People's Republic of China has been the effective government of mainland China. The regime is a revolutionary regime, the result of a very genuine revolution, and I suggest it is very hard for contemporaries to look at such revolutions with historic perspective and with detachment.
The cost of revolutions runs high, not only in lives but in human passions. Revolutions are often ruthless, particularly in the phase in which the revolutionaries fear counter-revolution and suspect that such counter-revolution will be aided by external force. The French and Russian revolutions are evidence of this, and the Chinese revolution is no exception.

Revolutions are often fanatical and selfrighteous. They claim a monopoly of the truth, but it is a mistake to spring from this to the conclusion that China is committed to world conquest. In fact, many of the most scholarly observers of the Chinese scene are convinced that this policy of China is based less on ideology and more on the history and traditions of China; its nationalistic ambitions and grievances.
China has suffered from a long period of humiliation from the western world. There is no need to detail here the history of crushing defeats in war, unequal treaties, foreign concessions and extra territoriality for foreigners. If we exercise any imagination at all, we should not be surprised to find, now that China is growing in strength, that it should express itself in bitter and uncompromising self-reliance. I suggest it would be wrong to go from this observation to a conclusion that western policy should be based upon containing communism and isolating one quarter of the world. Unfortunately, there are powerful governments, notably the government of the United States, which seem to base their policies unon the necessity of containing Commun'sm. It follows from that that they believe in the isolation of the People's Republic of China from diplomatic and other contacts with the western world.
It is our conviction, shared I believe by many members of this house, that this approach is a fatal mistake which sets the western world, particularly the United States of America and China, upon a collision course. It creates and at the same time feeds upon the view that war is inevitable. A wiser judgment is that when revolutionary regimes gain power they, like other human institutions, change in the course of time.
The men who made the revolution are nearly always intolerant and suspicious, but they grow in confidence and security. The practical problems of administering a new order bring to the fore new and less revolutionary and less isolationist groups of governors. On the other hand, enforced isolation prolongs the revolutionary era. It is not fanciful to attribute the Stalinist excesses in Russia to the indirect result of intervention and isolation of the U.S.S.R. Continued isolation of China may well play into the hands of Chinese extremists and might well postpone the day when more moderate elements will be ready to rejoin the world.
It is for these reasons that we warmly welcome the fact that at long last the Secretary of
Supply-External Affairs State for External Affairs, speaking for Canada at the United Nations, has proposed that the People's Republic of China should take the place of the National Republic of China in the general assembly and on the security council of the United Nations. This is a recognition of reality. For 17 years now, mainland China has been firmly governed by the present regime. The pretense that the Nationalist Republic of China controls China is clearly an empty sham which in no way corresponds with the realities. There is no sense in hoping that the future peace of the world can be based upon perpetuating a situation which is based upon such a sham.
It seems quite useless to talk about a two-China policy which accepts the claim of the Nationalist Republic of China, which now controls Formosa, to have control over China as a whole. Indeed, such a view would perpetuate the myth that there is some real prospect that by means of counter-revolution the nationalist regime may take control of China. The Chiang Kai-shek regime itself does not recognize the two China concept. We, in this party, are prepared to recognize the fact that the nationalist Chiang Kai-shek regime controls the island of Formosa. We think that if this regime seeks admission to the United Nations general assembly on this basis, the fact of its control of Formosa should be recognized and it should be admitted on that basis.
Admittedly it may not be possible for many years, but when it is possible the people of Formosa should be given an opportunity to determ no their own destiny. It may well be that the present regime in Taiwan would be unwilling to accept a place in the United Nations on this basis. In other words, it would be unwilling to give up its claim to speak for China as a whole, but I suggest the fact that it controls the island of Formosa is the only factual basis upon which it is entitled to sit at the United Nations. If the regime there does not choose to accept this position, that is its own affair. It should not be permitted to hold up, by a claim which no longer is real, the acceptance within the community of nations of the government which in fact has clearly demonstrated its control over the mainland of China.
We believe that the government of Canada must follow up its first step by further action. The government of Canada cannot of course control the decision of the United Nations or the views of its allies, but it should have the courage of its convictions and should now

That step is to afford diplomatic recognition. I suggest it would not only be hypocrit cal to do so, but it would appear to be hypocritical and would destroy all of the benefits that may flow from the in Dative the government has undertaken in the United Nations.

Let me pass from the subject, Mr. Chairman, to a closely related subject, the continued acceleration of the war in Viet Nam. It is not necessary for me to repeat the view that members of this party have advanced from time to time. This view has been that the involvement of the United States in that war is and has been a tragic mistake which is endangering the whole world and is, in fact, defeating the vital interests of the United States itself.
In the present context all that is necessary to be said is that since we last discussed this matter in th;s house this war has continued to escalate. I heard on the air today that the United States now has about 380,000 troops involved. It is continuing a massive and expanded program of bombing North Viet Nam with which it is not formally at war. There is no end to this tragic conflict in sight, certainly not from the military point of view. The escalation has not reached the possible end of its course. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition referred to the 100,000 Chinese troops on the border. They have not been used, thank God; but perhaps with a further escalation of the war they may come into action.

Then, we will have tragedy compounded on tragedy.

We have expressed our view that in so far as United States involvement has been based upon a theory that Chinese Communism must be contained, this is a mistake. We disagree not only with the basic theory but with the effectiveness of the method sought to be used to contain Commun.sm, the escalation of the war in Viet Nam, which is likely to produce precisely the opposite result.
The real problem at the present time is not what were the causes of the war, but how to put an end to hostilities. It is perfectly obvious that there is no way to do this except through a process of negotiation. The key issue, therefore, is how can the process of negotiation be init.ated and brought to a successful conclusion? The Secretary of State for External Affairs recently visited Poland the U.S.S.R. and Italy, and also spoke to His Holiness the Pope. No doubt in recent days he has been in close contact with the Secretary General of the United Nations, whose efforts to bring about negotiations are well known.
I ask the government spokesmen-indeed I ask the r.ght hon. Prime Minister-to tell this house very frankly whether or not all of these governments and authorities have not expressed to our representatives and our government a clear view that a necessary preliminary to negotiation is that the United States of America should cease the bombing of North Viet Nam. I ask whether or not the Canadian government is willing to associate itself clearly and unequivocally with this view. Has the government said, or will it say, to the United States of America that Canada advises this step, namely the cessation of bomb ng, be taken in the interests of peace? If such advice has been given, will it be given publicly and openly?
In the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs the other day on his return from his recent trip, he referred to what he called certain oversimplified suggestions that were being put forward. He included in these so-called oversimplified suggestions the proposal for unilateral decision, presumably by the United States, to stop the bombing of North Viet Nam, with no indication of what the other side might do in return. In these words, the minister appears to be adopting the view put forward by the administration of the United States that before it stops the bombing of North Viet Nam it must have assurances of the withdrawal of

North Vietnamese units from South Viet Nam.
I suggest that this is an impossible condition. The involvment of North Vietnamese units in South Viet Nam is by no means to be equated with the American bombing of North Viet Nam. After all, the Geneva agreement does not recogn ze the existence of North and South V.et Nam as separate entities, but has stated that there is a temporary line of demarcation between them.
It has been the contention of the National Liberation Front of the North Vietnamese that what in effect is taking place is a civil war. A parallel to the United States demand that the North Vietnamese units be withdrawn from South Viet Nam before the United States ceases the bombing would be the demand of Hanoi that the United States withdraw their forces from South Viet Nam before they will negotiate. This is a demand which indeed has been made, but is equally quite unrealistic, we all agree, if genuine negotiations are to take place.
I know it is said that the bombing of North Viet Nam is a necessary military action. Its results to date certainly do not appear to have demonstrated its efficacy. In any event-and in this, at least, I agree with the right hon. Leader of the Opposition-the political importance of an end rather than a continuance of the war makes it essential that political considerations predominate over purely military considerations.
It is also stated from time to time that the United States has proposed negotiations, only to have them consistently turned down by Hanoi. This version of the facts is all too simple. The fact of the matter is that there have been continued escalations of the military effort by the United States, which have frustrated the possiblity of fruitful negotiations. It was shortly after Mr. Ronning returned from Hanoi and reported to the government here, and through them to Mr. Harriman for the United States administration, that a further United States escalation of the war took place in the bombing of Hanoi and Haiphong in the north.
The government has first-hand information from Hanoi, through Mr. Ronning, as to whether or not it is hopeless to contemplate negotiations with Hanoi. The government knows whether of not, in fact, it was the attitude of Hanoi or the further escalation of the war by the United States that frustrated the prospect of negotiations at that time.
What we have urged is that this government put its full weight behind the almost

Supply-External Affairs universal plea that the United States should once again seek the road of negotiation by a cessation of bombing. This would it seems to us, do more than anything else that Canada could do to end this tragic war. May I say, Mr. Chairman, that I do not believe our involvement in the International Control Commission is any reason why, on this vital issue, we should not express our views clearly and forthrightly.
I do not have time to expand upon the steps necessary to build a world community by more strenuous efforts to end the growing gap between the poverty of what might be called the "slum areas" of the world and the complacent "suburb", which includes Canada. In this party we differ sharply in our view of priorities in building a world community. We believe the time has come for a dynamic new stance on Canada's contribution to defence and international affairs. We think Canada is in a position to make clear that its defence contribution will be primarly available to support peace keeping and the growth of the rule of law within the ambit of the United Nations. This will involve a change in the present dispositions within NATO. The government appears to have adopted a static policy in this respect; it has not told this house very much about any changes that it proposes.
We believe that a substantially increased contribution by Canada to economic aid is called for, and that the present effort is just not good enough. Perhaps other occasions will enable us to expand, and give in detail, our views on these matters.
I had not intended in these remarks to touch on the question of Rhodes;a. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition did so. I will content myself by saying to the Prime Minister-and I think I speak on behalf of my party-that we will support the government in the imposing and enforcing, so far as Canada can do so, of effective sanctions on the illegal reg'me in Rhodesia. We will be happy to do so, either at the request of the United Kingdom government, which is the legal sovereign in that country, or through action at the United Nations.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
We believe it is absolutely essential to maintain confidence not only in the United Nations but in the good faith of the western world and indeed of the Commonwealth. It should be made quite clear that the gestures we are making to bring this illegal regime to an end are not intended to be empty gestures or gestures which will be ineffective, but are

Supply-External Affairs designed to establish a legal regime, one which will not be based upon a colour bar or racial discrimination.
The Leader of the Opposition asked some questions on this subject. We do not ask questions; we are stating to the Prime Minister that we will support the government in any action that it takes in support of international law and the interests, of the world community.
May I conclude by saying that we in this party believe there are not only changes in detail required in our external policy, but also changes in the style and tone of Canada's contribution. We do not mean by this that Canada should repudiate its alliances or try to assume in international affairs a weight or importance that its power and position does not justify. We believe there is no doubt an important place for quiet diplomacy and for the influence which may be exercised, particularly in Washington, by means of such quiet diplomacy. However, we believe that the Canadian government owes it to the Canadian people, and more particularly to the younger people of Canada, to take a more vigorous and independent line on the great issues which are facing the world.
We welcome the new initiative taken in the United Nations by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on behalf of this government. It indicates a change in attitude and that we should be ready to put up with some criticism and coolness on the part of any of our allies who disagree with us. It is not enough today, if we are to have any pride in Canada's contribution as a nation, to be right or enlightened, as it were behind closed doors; we must be seen to be right and enlightened. I think that very often Canada's policies in this field are right and enlightened, but it is very d.fficult for the Canadian people to discern this in the miasma of words and ambiguities that often seem to shroud our policies.
In our view, Mr. Chairman, this does not mean that the conduct of our diplomacy should be a matter of emotional declamation. It means a continued and outspoken concentration an all these policies which we believe to be vital to the building of a world community and to a reconciliation between nations.

Mr. Chairman, it is a privilege to be able to take part in this brief debate on external affairs, as a discussion of the estimates of this department permits us to do at this time. I am grateful to the hon. member for Greenwood for disassociating myself from
tMr. Brewin.]
the policies that he tried to enunciate. I respect his sincerity as a friend, but I fail to follow his logic.
However, while one might disagree with what should be Canada's external affairs policies, there is some satisfaction in at least knowing the policies in which he believes. As I listened to the Leader of the Opposition, I found it very difficult to determine just what were the policies of his party as they related to some of the major problems he discussed.
In the limited time at my disposal, I propose to limit my remarks to two specific areas of foreign affairs. First of all, I should like briefly to discuss NATO. It has been my privilege, along with 14 or 15 other members of this house and the other place, to take part in the recent NATO parliamentarians conference in Paris. That conference gave us the opportunity of visiting and seeing at first hand our own NATO forces in Europe and of talking with both officers and men. We saw the job they were doing, the problems they faced and were made conscious of the purpose of their being there. At the end of the conference we had a brief one-day visit to the free city of Berlin.
I point with considerable pride to the fact that the parliamentarians conference in Paris this year saw it change from an annual conference to some semblance of a permanent body. At the conference it was decided to transform the annual parliamentary conference into a permanent north Atlantic assembly, and hereafter the annual meeting will be just that. As the responsibilities and powers of this new north Atlantic assembly take shape, I think you will see for the first time a very definite organization, made up of parliamentarians and other representatives from the 15 member nations of NATO, which will assume a greater role in policy and decision-making.
I also draw to the attention of the house the fact that the president of this first north Atlantic assembly is a Canadian, the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska. In view of the fact that the concept of a parliamentarians conference was originally largely due to the vision and efforts of a great Canadian, who served as first president of the former organization, we now have the honour of being the country to supply the first president of the new organization. I am sure I am expressing the goodwill and opinions of all members of this house when I say that this is truly another indication that Canada is growing up and is playing a bigger and bigger role in this ever-narrowing world community of nations.

With regard to the position of NATO at the present time, despite the difficulties that have been caused by the withdrawal of France from the integrated military command, the role and purpose of NATO is even greater than before. I think this is realized particularly by our own personnel who serve NATO; and in this regard more than 11,000 of our armed forces are serving in France and Germany today. The men of the three air wings, and the brigade serving with them, are not only doing a tremendous job as ambassadors of Canada, but represent a great devotion and dedication to purpose so far as peace in Europe is concerned. They certainly play a very major part in maintaining the peace of the world.
I also say that the role of NATO is changing. This factor was a basic topic of discussion in the various committees at the parliamentarians conference. No one will deny that NATO's role is changing. Whatever was the motivation and reason for France's military withdrawal, it has precipitated a more rapid change in the role of NATO than ever. It was brought to our attention by the Secretary General of NATO and others that there is still a continuing military role for NATO in Europe. We talk of a detente and we hear a good deal spoken of the new softer relationships between east and west. This is good and we are grateful for every bit of ground that is gained.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
However, the Secretary General of NATO brought to our attention that the armed forces of communist nations, under one direct command, have increased during the last year by some 40 per cent on the eastern side of the iron curtain; that today, facing the NATO military forces in Germany and France are more than 2 million communist troops at combat readiness, and that the armaments of those troops include nuclear arms. Also it was pointed out that particularly those nuclear arms, and he refers to missiles, have increased by 50 per cent in the last three years. It is wishful thinking for anybody to say that the time has come for the military withdrawal of NATO altogether. This is wishful thinking so long as communist forces continue to build up on the eastern side of the iron curtain.
Those who have had the privilege of visiting Berlin and seeing the wall of shame -incidentally it has been completely rebuilt and modernized into a permanent structure-will understand that the division of Germany is complete and the basic problem of
Supply-External Affairs peace in Europe is a long way from being settled. As against that, a most significant development of our parliamentarian's conference this year came about in the special committee of underdeveloped NATO nations. Specifically, I refer to Greece and Turkey. The delegates from Greece and Turkey, both leading parliamentarians in their own countries, sat on either side of the chairman of this committee. Both men agreed that relations between their two countries have improved a great deal in recent months, as evidenced by the four economic projects developed as a result of the committee. That is most encouraging. Those four projects relate to the development of irrigation and hydroelectric projects along the river forming their common boundary; to their common interests in tourism, an important industry in those ancient countries; to the development of markets for vegetables and other products of those countries, and to the improvement of their own exports and balance of payments.
In other areas it was seen that NATO ties are very important economically, as well as militarily. One cannot emphasize the importance of these ties which were strengthened by the parliamentarians of NATO countries getting together to discuss the solutions to the problems existing between the two nations, to which I have referred. The two countries mentioned have the focal point of their troubles in Cyprus, where thousands of our Canadian boys are serving as peacekeepers between them.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that any money this country spends on its NATO commitments, whether those be for the defensive role on the military side of NATO or on the political, scientific or cultural side, or for special projects such as the committee I have referred to, is money well spent. I underline the fact that those who say it is time for NATO to disappear, that NATO has fulfilled its purpose and that NATO has been destroyed by France, are completely wrong. I say, Mr. Chairman, and I am talking about NATO, that the next conference, the first meeting of the new North Atlantic assembly, should be held in Canada. I ask the Prime Minister whether this could not be done. The president of the North Atlantic assembly wishes an invitation to be extended for the first session of the new assembly to be held in Canada next fall. It is only reasonable that the assembly should come here, because a Canadian is president of it; also, because it is necessary to move the headquarters of NATO and SHAPE to Belgium, accommodation will

Supply-External Affairs not be ready tor the parliamentarians' conference, and we should render NATO a service if an invitation could be extended to hold the first North Atlantic assembly here.
This would fit in with Canada's developing role in national affairs. It would show genuinely that we do have a role to play in world affairs. I hope the Prime Minister will consider seriously what I ask. I suggest also to the Prime Minister that what I have said is an adequate reason for the committee on external affairs to assemble immediately. I believe positive issues can be considered by that committee. It need not become involved in the major issues of the world, but I hope that an invitation to the new North Atlantic assembly will be the first item on the new agenda.
I regret that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is not with us. It is difficult to have any real debate on external affairs without his presence, particularly when one remembers recent developments in Europe and at the United Nations.
Preceding the NATO conference, the Secretary of State for External Affairs visited Poland and Moscow. I will not take time to discuss the reported reasons for that visit, nor the objectives which might have been gained by it. I assume that in Poland most of the conversation centred around the role of Canada and Poland on the international truce commission. None the less, some reports coming out of Moscow, and some reasons which have been given for the trip being made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, are disturbing. I say that particularly because of the remarks I have made about NATO. The objectives of Stalin and Khrushchev were to weaken and destroy NATO. There was great rejoicing in Moscow, when General de Gaulle visited there, over the role France had played in recent months in NATO. No one can doubt that the action of France greatly weakened the effectiveness of NATO, albeit what has happened may prove the starting point of a complete overhaul of the functions and objectives of NATO in the changing situation in Europe.
What happened next was that the Secretary of State for External Affairs decided to go to Moscow. It seems to me, as has already been said in the press, the minister is playing a rather curious and dangerous game. You will recall that prior to his departure there were reports that a member of our own civil service was involved in espionage. This espionage has since been brought to light. We understand that the espionage consisted of the giving of

certain vital and important maps of our east coast to the U.S.S.R.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
This is not an isolated case. It is reported that the U.S.S.R. is of the opinion that we carry on anti-Soviet campaigns in Canada, though the visit of the deputy premier should have eliminated that idea. Nevertheless, there has been persistent espionage activity in this country by Russia which claims now to be our special friend and a country with whom we are enjoying ever closer relations. We do want closer friendships with every country of the world and I believe that the Chinese situation, as it affects the Soviet Union, w.ll inevitably draw Russia closer to the western world. But let us not deceive ourselves into thinking that Russia's present policy of co-existence with Canada and the western world is as innocent as some Canadians seem to believe. The more contacts we have with that country the better, but let us keep both eyes open in assessing the objectives of the present policy of coexistence which is probably no more nor less than an expression of the attitude the Soviet Union has always taken toward the spread of international communism, only without the use of military force.
We cannot go much further into these developments in the time available to us. I mentioned the visit to Russia of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the light of the pronouncement by Canada at the United Nations in the last few days of what is, apparently, a new Canadian policy. Undoubtedly this policy was discussed during the visit to Moscow. Similarly, I have no doubt, it was discussed with Italian representatives during the visit to Italy. Now, we see it made public at the United Nations.
What has now become evident to all Canadians is a fact which many of us have been suspecting for some while: a complete change in Canadian policy is now taking place. If we turn our thoughts back to November 28, 1963, we will find that speaking in this chamber the Secretary of State for External Affairs clearly enunciated government policy on some of these major issues. Referring specifically to China; he said: "We have had a recent example of China taking the initiative to intensify her own isolation." The hon. gentleman was obviously convinced that it was China which was isolating itself from the world, not the world which was isolating China.

Further on in his policy statement the hon. gentleman said:
The avowed intention of Peking to occupy Formosa stands as a serious obstacle to both the seating of Communist China in the United Nations at this time and to the recognition of the Peking regime.
On May 22, 1964, the secretary of state had a great deal more to say about Canadian policy toward Communist China. But it was on November 17, 1965, that the hon. gentleman made the most comprehensive statement about problems concerned with Red China-one of the clearest statements he has ever made, in my opinion, on this aspect of policy. If one compares the statements made in this speech of November 12 with the statement which was made in the United Nations a couple of days ago one finds there has been a complete reversal of the Canadian attitude toward this issue. I do not believe Communist China has changed her ideas. Looking at the reports which come out of China I get the impression that Chinese policy is unchanged except that it is being pursued with a higher degree of intensity than ever before. Since China has not altered her policy, it must be that Canadian policy has changed.
In 1965 the Secretary of State for External Affairs outlined his reasons for not voting in the United Nations for the seating of Red China. Now, he says Red China must be seated. I agree it would be ideal if Red China could enter the United Nations on the same terms, in accordance with the charter, as every other member. World tension would be greatly relieved if, somehow, the two Chinas could be made to understand that both should have a seat and that Red China, because of her size, should, logically, have a seat on the Security Council.
But what the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said on this subject amounts, in my opinion, to wishful thinking -talking to the wind for some purpose which I do not understand. I say this because Red China has evidently no intention of accepting the terms of the United Nations charter and no intention of recognizing the fact that the 12 million people who live on Taiwan have as much right to representation as large numbers of other states which have been admitted recently without questions asked.
Further, it is obvious that at the present neither the United Nations nor any group of nations within that organization, is keeping Red China out of the UN. It is Red China herself who is responsible for the present position. Talk about universality is all very well,
Supply-External Affairs but there must be qualifications, and those qualifications are inherent in the terms of the charter itself. Until Red China is willing to take her seat on the same conditions as affect every other nation, there can be no question about her admission. Yet at a time when even communist nations are on the verge of withdrawing recognition from Red China because it has been impossible for them to get along with her, we find Canada running behind that nation and pleading with her to come in-for what purpose, I am not sure.
Even while the Secretary of State for External Affairs was in Europe a memorandum was circulated to some 40 nations, I think, outlining the action Canada intended to take. Yet Italy-and some people say we were outmanoeuvred-came forward with a resolution which, it seems to me, embodied a more realistic approach than the one suggested by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his speech made the day before yesterday.
As I have said on a number of occasions it is impossible to separate economic affairs from defence policy or foreign policy. Perhaps the reason Canada is adopting her present course is simply that she has permitted herself to enter into trading relations with Red China without counting the full cost which is bound to be felt on the political side.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Before concluding this discussion, Mr. Chairman, I wish to say it is imperative that in forming a policy with regard to Red China we must face the reality of the situation as it exists, and look with a practical eye to the future. It follows from the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the United Nations that if Canada is to maintain her honour before the rest of the world, she must seek to establ sh and maintain diplomatic relations with Red China. How will this benefit Canada?
Great Britain has had diplomatic relations with Red China since 1949, even though she has not been able to maintain an embassy at Peking, and merely is served by a charge d'affaires. What benefit has this been to Great Britain in so far as handling the problems created by Red China are concerned? It might be that we should continue to use the good will that we have throughout the world, and in the United Nations, to try to bring together those who take an obstinate stand on this problem, so that they may be persuaded to work out some sort of agreed policy. Until that can be done any talking that we do now is just so much smoke in the wind.

As recently as today it has been reported that some of Red China's immediate neighbours, like Japan and Indonesia, disagree completely with Canada's present approach. I hope that we will give support to the Italian resolution and at the same time continue to use our good will, without making fools of ourselves, in an effort to solve this problem. I agree it is a problem that must be solved. We cannot expect to have world peace until it is, but we must approach its solution on principle, facing the realities, with practical reasoning behind the policies that we develop.
Our new policy on this matter is a complete reversal of our policy just a year ago, and this is difficult to understand. If the reasons given in November, 1965, for the policy we had then were valid, then they invalidate what has been said by the Secretary of State for External Affairs within the last few days.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, there is one overriding factor that I would like to see become a part of our role in world affairs. It is that we over shadow all others in our possession of know-how, and in actual production, as the food basket of the world. Those of us who know India are especially concerned to read of the tremendous famine problem which that country faces, to read that literally millions of people are going to starve to death within the next month because they have no food. The problem of world food production seems to worsen year by year. The rich get richer and the have-not nations have less and less.
One of Canada's principal tasks should be to move forward, not only in sharing the wealth we have but also in sharing the know-how we have. We should be using our good will to formulate a new policy that will help meet the basic problem of all mankind, that of having enough food in order to survive. Instead of wasting our time on some matters upon which we cannot expect to have very much influence-

Instead of wasting our time, instead of advancing policies which are contrary to our former policies which I believe were and are sound, instead of wandering out into water that is way beyond our depth, we should be providing an answer to some of the basic problems of human beings. Mr. Chairman, we are discussing the estimates of the Department of External Affairs under a rule, approved by all parties in the house, that there should be a limitation imposed of a certain number of days for supply discussions. That is the reason we have not perhaps as much time as we would have liked to have had to spend on this very important subject today. However, Mr. Chairman, I point out that there have been a good many discussions of external affairs in this parliament and in the standing committee on external affairs. I venture to say that if the record were looked up it would show that there was as much consideration given to external affairs in this parliament as in any previous parliament, in respect of general foreign policy matters.
I would like also to point out that when we discuss external affairs and we, as a government, are criticized for not informing the House of Commons in advance of the positions we are taking at the United Nations General Assembly on certain issues, or in respect of diplomatic discussions that are going on with other countries, we are following a traditional parliamentary practice of conducting negotiations, as a government must conduct negotiations at times with other governments, in confidence. The principles on which those negotiations should be conducted are principles which should be stated to parliament, and within those principles diplomatic arrangements and diplomatic discussions are carried on and, when a government takes a position as a result of these discussions then, naturally it stands or falls on that position.
I have been looking up the record with regard to information given to parliament before meetings of General Assemblies in the past on the question of Chinese representation, and I find that this certainly was the practice in those years before 1963-
But only after discussion in parliament.

I did not want to spend much time on this point, Mr. Chairman, but it looks as if I should give some detail, having made the statement. Before the United Nations General Assembly met in 1958 there was no report made to the House of Commons by the then secretary of state for external affairs in regard to the question of China, which was on

the United Nations agenda; there was no report made in 1959 before the General Assembly discussed the question of Chinese representation, and there was no report made before the General Assembly meeting of 1960.
In 1961, the prime minister of that day was asked about Canadian policy on September 20, just after the General Assembly met, and he said he was not able to go into detail beyond saying that the question was a very important one and that the people of Taiwan should have the right to decide their own future.
The stand taken by the government at that time was made known in the United Nations, and parliament then had the responsibility, if it so desired, to decide whether or not that was a right stand. That is the traditional parliamentary practice. I think it is well that parliament should discuss external affairs matters both in committee and in committee of the whole house. I think the record of the last three or four years in that regard has been a good one. I call attention to the number of times the standing committee on external affairs met when the question of China and its relationship to the United Nations has come up, and also the number of times when it has come up in the House of Commons.

I think China is the subject that I should deal with first because it is one that has been touched upon, and in some cases more than touched upon, by those speakers representing the various parties who have preceded me. It has been suggested that the answers which have been given to questions in the House of Commons recently have been definitely misleading. I do not accept that statement, Mr. Chairman, and I think that if the statement made yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs is examined in detail by those who are interested, they will find that what has been said in the House of Commons is not in contradiction to what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in New York yesterday. The Canadian position in respect of this very important matter of the representation of China at the United Nations I believe was very clearly outlined in the statement made yesterday. The Secretary of State for External Affairs-and I wish he were here to speak on this matter himself; perhaps no one wishes this more than I do-outlined the essentials which we would consider would constitute a reasonable solution to this problem. I know it is difficult to formulate an important matter in a word, but in a word the proposal

Supply-External Affairs was that the governments of both the Republic of China and the People's Republic of China should be represented in the General Assembly in respect of the territories under their effective jurisdictions and that the government of the People's Republic of China should be the permanent member on the Security Council representing the territory over which it effectively has had jurisdiction for 15 or more years now and which includes 700 million people.
The position embodied in the minister's statement was framed specifically to avo.d interference in what must be considered as internal Chinese affairs and in particular to avo.d pre-judging the question of China's being a s.ngle sovere.gn entity, as both Ch.nese governments cla m at the present time. Of course we know this. Therefore, this proposal or suggestion is not an attempt to create two Ch.nas; it is an attempt to outl.ne what m.ght be a reasonable interim solution to the problem of Chinese representation, strictly limited to the United Nations context, with no implications in respect of the questions of sovere gnty or territorial rights which one day will have to be settled by the Ch nese themselves including those who live on Taiwan. That was the purpose of the statement. The pol cy embodied in that statement has been given to th s house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and indeed by myself on more than one occasion. It is a pol.cy based on the desirab 1 ty of universality in a world organization. In that statement of yesterday we have not abandoned the belief that the policy of universal ty should be implemented in such a way that it would not expel a present member government from the United Nations.
In making that statement and in outlining this policy the objective was to begin, and we hoped it would begin, a process of breaking the log jam which has faced the United Nations assembly for many years. We hoped it might produce some ideas which might result in some progress be'ng made in dealing with the matter of representat on of Ch na wh ch is on the agenda of the United Nations, as it has been now year after year for more than 15 years. I believe the statement which has been made w'll have a helpful effect in that direction. I hope that it will result in other motions being made at the United Nations General Assembly in the form of new and positive approaches to at least an examination of this problem with a view to finding a solution.
Before the United Nations assembly at present there are three resolutions which deal with the question of Chinese representation.

November 24. 1966
Supply-External Affairs There is the resolution which comes up every year, and this is the one which I hope will be decided first, to decide whether or not this question is an important one within the meaning of the rules of procedure of the United Nations. If it is considered to be a question of great substance-and I cannot imagine a question of much greater importance-it then would require a two thirds majority. That is important. This is one resolution. Then there is the perennial Albanian resolution which provides for the admission of the government of Peking, and at the same time for the expulsion from the United Nations of the government of Taiwan.
When the Secretary of State for External Affairs issued his statement on Chinese representation in November 1965, he was deal-ig with the Albanian resolution and explaining why we would not support it at that time. We do not propose to support it this year either, because we cannot vote for a resolution which in its terms would expel the government of Taiwan from the United Nations. Presumably this resolution will come up early next week for decision. There will be the same reluctance, and indeed impossibility on our part, to support a resolution in those terms.
Then, there is a third resolution put forward by the Italian, Belgian, Chilean, and I think one or two other, delegations which provides for an examination of the matter by a committee which would report back to the United Nations assembly a year from now. In its terms, it is almost the same kind of resolution which the Canadian delegation put forward in 1950 without very much success.
We appreciate the desire of the sponsors of this resolution to join us and others in making a step forward and in making some progress in this matter. We feel it is a satisfactory resolution so far as it goes, but we do not feel that it goes far enough to ensure that at the end of the year's examination we shall be faced at the next meeting of the assembly with a realistic and helpful report on this matter which could lead to further desirable action. That is the reason the Secretary of State for External Affairs made a statement yesterday and proposed an examination of the question, not in the form of a resolution but rather in the form of a suggestion put forward for consideration and discussion. In this form it goes somewhat further than the Italian resolution, because it lays down certain guide lines-if I may use that word-which would influence the examination which is
about to be made. It suggested that that examination should not be carried on by a committee of the assembly, because it would be difficult indeed to get a satisfactory committee. The suggestion was that this be carried out by the president of the assembly himself, with all the help he can get from the many sources available to him and particularly from the Secretary General of the United Nations.
This proposal which was put forward yesterday embodied a policy which goes a long way back before this session of the general assembly. I believe it will continue after this assembly rises. It is not embodied in a resolution. Had we made this suggestion in the form of a resolution-and we had been considering that right up until the last few days-it might have been, and indeed I think it would have been, defeated by a large majority as going too far for some and not far enough for others. With the Italian resolution which is on the order paper providing for an examination, such a proposal by Canada might have received an inadequate number of votes and, that particular kind of a proposal having been defeated in the form of a resolution, it might have been more difficult to resurrect later. However, in the form of the proposal as made in a statement by the Canadian delegation, it is now open for discussion and consideration.

More than one speaker this afternoon has asked how the government of Peking and its policies have changed so as to warrant the Canadian delegation putting toward a proposal of this kind at this time. There is no one who can be optimistic, in the light of events, that it would be possible to find any resolution which would be acceptable to the Peking government except one in the terms of the Albanian resolution, which we could not support because of its expulsion clause. We have no illusions about that and we have no illusions that Peking's policy has suddenly changed or that the government of Peking by any change would suddenly become eligible for participation in the United Nations as a peace-loving nation within the terms of its charter. If one applied that standard literally to all the members of the United Nations today, or to the nations who may apply in future, I do not know how many members of the United Nations would be able to subscribe to such terms without some qualification.
The question is not whether the policies of the government of Peking have suddenly changed in a way that makes it an acceptable

November 24, 1966

representative at the United Nations which has no revolutionary or aggressive instincts, or that it has suddenly abandoned certain policies which could hardly be called peace-loving. That is not the question which faces the United Nations at this time. The question is whether or not the United Nations is going to take its responsibility in doing its best to see that a suitable basis can be found in that world assembly so that a government which represents effectively 700 million people in this world can be represented in that organization. We will discharge our responsibility as a member of the United Nations if we try to find a basis of negotiation with Peking. Having done that, it will be up to Peking to made a dicision. It may well be that the government of Peking will spurn, as indeed it has already given some indication it will, this kind of offer to find a basis on which membership could be granted. The United Nations and its members will have discharged this reponsibil-ity if an effort is made to find such a basis for membership. That is the purpose of the examination that has been proposed by the Italian and other delegates, and it is the purpose of the proposals that have been put forward by our Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Let me now move from China and its representation at the United Nations to the second subject which has been referred to this afternoon. I should like to deal with the question of Viet Nam and southeast Asia. There is no more important matter on the international scene at this time, nor one more fraught with immediate danger to general peace in that area.
It is very discouraging, but realistic, to note that since the house last discussed foreign affairs there has been no movement in Viet Nam which brings us any closer to a peaceful settlement. Despite repeated attempts to find a basis for peace talks, the problem in Viet Nam is still being tackled today as a military problem. We have made clear our belief, and I know this house shares this belief because hon. members have made that clear this afternoon, that the removal of this source of serious instability in southeast Asia-that is putting it mildly-will not be achieved by military means alone. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition has emphasized this fact.
It is precisely because we are convinced of the need for a political solution that we have made every effort within our power to see whether we could help in finding a basis for a political solution. That is also the reason we
Supply-External Affairs have welcomed the repeated expressions of the United States' willingness to enter into negotiations leading to a lasting settlement. That is also why we are discouraged and disappointed that there has been no expression of such intention, desire or willingness on the part of the government of North Viet Nam, which is certainly a party to this conflict.
While I can understand the difficulty of the government of North Viet Nam relating any kind of movement toward peace to the bombing of its territory or, as long as the bombing of its territory is going on, to talk about a peace movement, I find it very difficult to understand why that government has refused to accept missions, including the mission of commonwealth prime ministers, which desire to discuss with that government the basis upon which some kind of peaceful negotiation could be brought about. The mission I mention consisted of prime ministers of countries not unfriendly to the North Vietnamese side of this case, and none committed to the United States side. That has been very discouraging indeed.
Who were those prime ministers besides Nkrumah?

They included the man who was then representing Ghana, President Nkrumah, the Prime Minister of Ceylon and the Prime Minister of Trinidad-Tobago, Dr. Eric Williams.
We have always held the view that the bombing of North Viet Nam was, and indeed remains, the key element in this dangerous military and diplomatic impasse. We have made that view known more than once in Washington and at least once in public in the United States. We have also made clear our belief that the bombing is unlikely to stop merely as a result of denunciatory declarations or appeals. Nor is any practical impact going to be made by an over-simplified and unrealistic prescription for peace which places on only one side the full burden of responsibility for making essential concessions.
I should like to hear a statement from Washington to the effect that bombing will stop, and I should like to hear a statement from Hanoi that if the bombing stops the infiltration of troops into South Viet Nam will stop. There are indications that this is the direction of United States policy statements. If there is any fear on the part of North Viet Nam, communists in North Viet Nam, in Peking, in Moscow or anywhere else that the
November 24. 1966

Supply-External Affairs United States will not withdraw from South Viet Nam after peace negotiations have begun, or perhaps brought to an end, I should like it made crystal clear that the United States has no intention of remaining in South Viet Nam. I believe that to be the case.
Would the Prime Minister permit a question? What was the reason for the United States imposition of the six month's rule? I do not understand that.

I should not like to try to explain the significance of that specific declaration. What I am trying to point out, and I am sure my right hon. friend and other members will agree with me, is that if the suspicion that the United States is going to stay indefinitely in Viet Nam can be removed, and if these powers can be convinced that the United States is there for one purpose, to support a government which it considers to be the victim of aggression, the situation might improve. If these people can be convinced that once this aggression, as the United States and South Viet Nam see it, has stopped, and once peace talks have started, that the process of withdrawal will begin, that South Viet Nam is not going to be a base for the United States, as I believe the United States does not wish it to be, and that the people as a result of peace talks will have the opportunity of deciding their destiny for themselves as a neutral power-if they so wish-I am sure the results will be beneficial.

I think it is important to remove any fear. We have discovered this fear in all the talks and discussions we have had with communist representatives. They say that the United States have not moved into the area with the forces they have, with the facilities they have brought in, with the work that has been done there-the building of harbours, and all that sort of thing-unless the United States are going to stay. If that fear could be removed, it would be a great step forward. There must be the removal of this fear if there is to be peace. The people of the area must also have the chance to vote freely as to what they want to do, and under what regime they want to live. If we could remove these fears, I think we would progress a long way on the road to peace. But that is a very big "if" indeed.
I do not think there is anything more I can usefully add at this time, except perhaps to repeat what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said the other day. In the talks we have had recently, and through his

visit to Moscow and Poland, we have found little for encouragement in so far as the prospect for immediate improvement in the situation is concerned. There are very great differences of view, for instance, between ourselves and other western countries and the Soviet union, though I believe the Soviet union is as anxious to bring this war to an end as we are. But they feel that this cannot be done unless the United States stops its bombing and fighting and begins to remove its troops. They say that at that time there will be the right kind of reaction from the north. The United States feels it should not be asked to take those steps unless there is some assurance that they will result in negotiation and peace. There is, of course, a very great difference between the kind of sanctions put into effect last year and the sanctions which would be put into effect if the security council agreed, to make them obligatory on all United Nations members. The right hon. gentleman said this course could not be effective unless those sanctions were extended to South Africa. I know this is a very great difficulty, and I suppose the United Kingdom knows even better that it is a very great difficulty.
I would only point out that if the United Nations and all its members were sincere in their desire to put into effect selective obligatory sanctions, and took the necessary steps to carry them out, it would be possible, by selecting certain key exports from Rhodesia, to do very great and perhaps crippling damage to the economy of that country, because it would be possible to police these sanctions in a way that was not possible in respect of the present sanctions. It would not be easy to export those commodities through South Africa, to members of the United Nations who were putting sanctions into effect, without the importing countries knowing that they came originally from Rhodesia, because in most cases they would know the commodities were not South African at all in their origin.
It is a question of whether the United Nations wishes to take this step and whether the members of the United Nations fall behind it and do their best to make it work. If they do not do this, these sanctions will not work either, if they are put into effect. The hon. member for Red Deer spoke of the NATO assembly which had been meeting in Paris, and I should like to echo his tribute and congratulations to the hon. member for Res-tigouche-Madawaska for having been chosen the first president of the North Atlantic assembly.
I wish I had more time to discuss NATO, Mr. Chairman, but I have not. I know that the committee is anxious to get on with other business. But while we have been considering China, southeast Asia and Rhodesia we should not overlook the fact that a key area of the world remains eastern and western Europe, and that NATO remains a vital agency for peace and progress in that area through its provision of machinery for collective defence and for building up the Atlantic community.
Important changes are taking place in NATO. We who have believed in NATO from the beginning, as I know all members of this house have, should remember that what was exactly the right form of organization for 1949 is not necessarily the right form of organization for 1966. I think these changes will have to be reflected in the form and structure of NATO.
For one thing, Mr. Chairman, the European countries should be given or should take a greater share in the control and functioning of the collective defence organization. But if they are to do this, they will also have to take a greater share in responsibility too. I think that if we are to keep NATO going as an effective	organization-and I hope we
can-we will have to move toward a form of partnership between the North American side of NATO and the European side of NATO, both sides working together. We in NATO will also have to move away from the immediate military defensive side toward-and I hope this turns out to be the case-political discussion with eastern Europe and the countries behind the Iron Curtain.
We in NATO have been talking about this for the last ten years but have shied away from it. Some of its members have thought that this would be a sign of weakness or would be too defensive, but it is pretty well agreed now that a very important function of NATO is to establish contact with the other collective security organization in Eastern Europe. If this is to be done, then all members of NATO will have to work together, and this includes France.

I am sure no one regrets more than the members of this house the abandonment by France of its position in NATO so far as an integrated military organization is concerned. But France still remains a member of the organization, and we must do everything we can to see that she is given no reason for withdrawing from the political side of NATO. In the future, I hope that France may come back even into the military side of NATO. To be a member of a defence organization like NATO and to take part in collective defence but to say that you will not organize for collective defence until the emergency occurs, flies in the face of all history, especially modern history. So, I hope that perhaps even in that respect there may be developments which will strengthen NATO in the years ahead.
