speechtext:
The committee will now proceed with the estimates of the Department of Finance for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1967. These estimates are to be found at page 118 of the blue book.
DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE Administration-
1. Departmental administration including administration of the Guaranteed Loans Acts and the Inspector General of Banks' Office, and payments to provinces and grants as detailed in the Estimates, $4,332,900.

Mr. Chairman, it was interesting this afternoon hearing the Minister of Labour tell the house that he was receiving favourable comment from across the country on the announcement he made concerning the increased interest rate on mortgages. The information and news releases I have do not bear out his statement. It is true that the National House Build ng Association commends our interest, at last, in housing, but they are deeply concerned that the increased costs of funds will preclude people from buying homes. They call on the government to offset these difficulties through incentive programs.
The study of the estimates of the Minister of Finance gives us an opportunity to appraise the recent announcement by the Minister of Labour that the interest rate under the National Housing Act is hiked from 6J per cent to 7J per cent. To many people, at first glance, this hike is not unreasonable. But it is, after
November 24, 1966

all, an 8 per cent increase in the cost of borrowing for those who want to build a home. Add to this the 7 per cent increase of January, this year, and we see that the prospective home builder or owner is faced with a 15 per cent increase in interest rates on money for construction.
Can this government say to the Canadian people that this is truly realistic, when so many other factors should have been considered before the announcement was made? Does the increase in the rate of interest answer the serious problem with which the housing industry is confronted? Does it answer the plight of those prospective home owners who have searched in vain during the last 12 months for sources of money for mortgages? Notices, warnings and warning signals have been given to this government continually during the last year about the housing shortage and about the lack of mortgage funds. These warnings were ignored until recently, when Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation received authorization to increase direct loans. Unfortunately the extra allotment was not enough to meet all requests, and we have again had to resort to the normal supplies of mortgage money. Returns on normal mortgage moneys have been made more attractive. That action, in an industry that has been used as an instrument of economic leverage, with this government's policy of indifference, has placed many Canadian prospective home owners in a really sad position.
Through its policies, the government has subdued to a state of despair the lower and middle class wage earners who must buy shelter for their families. The cost of the average house is now out of proportion to the average salary, and we are adding extra costs by increasing interest charges, by increasing costs of building materials, by permitting high wages, and so on. Does the government believe that the 8 per cent increase in interest, plus the 7 per cent increase of January, will produce funds which will be invested in the housing industry?
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
If so, will it provide sufficient funds to meet the demands and requirements of the immediate future? Conventional mortgage rates are now running at approximately 8 per cent and the new rate set under the National Housing Act is certainly not likely to create a competitive market for housing mortgages. Do we not also acknowledge that the shortage of funds will in turn bring about shortage of housing 23033-652
Supply-Finance
units, and that the process of supply and demand will entail higher rental costs to be borne by those with whom we are mainly concerned-the lower and middle class wage earners? This latest decision is just another government contribution to the inflationary pressures which are haunting our economic welfare. It all adds up to action taken by an irresponsible government unaware of the problems of the common people.
Earlier, I mentioned that we seem to be witnessing the whittling down of various benefits and safeguards in the housing field. First of all, there was the government's refusal to eliminate the 11 per cent sales tax on building material. Second, there was the announcement that the $500 bonus for winter construction would no longer be granted. Now comes approval of this increase in the interest rate. It all amounts to a staggering cost burden on those who can ill afford to bear it.
Government policy must be flexible enough to be capable of adaptation to sudden and unexpected reactions. I believe that if home owners or intending home owners are obliged to pay additional costs in connection with their borrowing requirements, they should also receive the benefit of other measures whose effect would be to soften the blow. For example, why should not such people benefit immediately from a rebate of the 11 per cent sales tax? Why should it not be provided that school or municipal taxes be deductible for income tax purposes? Such an announcement, coming at this time of the year, would undoubtedly encourage prospective home owners to proceed with their construction projects provided funds were available.
The money market today is in an unstable and uncertain position largely as a result of the government's delay in bringing down the revisions to the Bank Act. It might have been possible to avoid the increase now contemplated in interest rates had the Bank Act in its revised form been passed by this house. Canadians will condemn this government for the priority which it has accorded to some legislation while delaying the progress of such essential legislation as the Bank Act.
We are of the opinion that mortgage moneys must ordinarily come from the private sector, but that when the private sector cannot meet the requirements of the population it becomes a duty of the state to enter any particular field of operations in order to fill the gap. If the government has been able to authorize lending at 6J per cent to home builders in the past, it should consider making

November 24, 1966
Supply-Finance
loans available once again at the same rate, if the private sector cannot meet the need. If this were done, some of the financial strain which home owners will experience as a result of this higher interest proposal would be alleviated.
We had that in our program.

Yes, I know. It is not an original suggestion. To me, it is rather strange that a person operating a business where property is involved is allowed to deduct his municipal taxes from income tax but the home owner does not have this benefit.
In recent days numerous newspaper articles have appeared indicating that the government should subsidize interest rates in Canada to provide mortgage money for house building at, say, 5 per cent. I contend that the government is, in effect subsidizing interest rates by guaranteeing mortgages under the National
November 24, 1966

Housing Act and that, in effect, people using that act are borrowing money cheaper than in the open market.
One of the areas in which the government is showing leadership is in the proposed amendments to the Bank Act, which are presently being considered by a committee of the house, whereby banks will be allowed to enter the mortgage field. They have been virtually restricted from doing so up until now because they were not allowed to charge more than 6 per cent. During the last two or three weeks that I have served on this committee I have learned from bankers that they are anxious to enter the residential mortgage field, and I feel this will help the situation.
There is a critical shortage of housing and it will continue into the near future. But this afternoon we listened to the Prime Minister outlining some of the problems that face the world. In the face of those problems we must consider ourselves very lucky to be Canadians. But I believe it is the responsibility of the government to manage the country's economy in such a way that we do not have booms or busts, so that we can level our booms and lift up the economy on a gradual, rising scale.
Interest rates around the world are high. Perhaps this is only a transitional period. Certainly, the experience in Canada has been that each time the interest rates go up they come down again, but they never come down to the point from where they started. The result has been that we have had a built-in, gradual inflationary effect in the area of interest rates. Perhaps we in Canada have been living under an artificial umbrella. Now as the rest of the world grows closer, and certainly as the commercial and banking worlds grow closer, world interest rates are going to affect Canadians. As we move into areas of free trade and accept more and more responsibility, both in peace keeping operations and in world trade, we will have to recognize that although a government never wants to raise interest rates, it may have to do so.
The Porter commission has pointed out that a government is always reluctant to raise interest rates, but I believe in this instance the government has accepted a principal recommendation of the Porter commission report. I feel that under this system, with the concept of a cabinet or government administering N.H.A. rates, for political reasons or otherwise-I do not suggest governments have been doing this-and with a free floating rate, over the long run mortgage money will 23033-652i
Supply-Finance
become more readily available because investors will invest their money in guaranteed N.H.A. loans.
Individuals have a freedom of choice as to where they are going to invest their dollars. When they have a reasonable degree of security they will invest their dollars where they feel they will earn the most return. If we believe in the free enterprise system, and if we have the necessary safeguards to protect against abuses, I believe this is what will provide the impetus to attract capital which will build more and better homes for Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, the debate we are now having arises out of the attempt made by the opposition yesterday to have a special debate on the announcement the Minister of Labour made about the increase in interest rates. It gives us an opportunity to comment on that announcement and express our views as to what the likely result will be.
I hope the minister will not take anything I say as aimed at him personally. I am no longer convinced, as I once was, that he is prepared to fight for an effective housing program, but I realize many of the constitutional difficulties which lie in the way. I shall come back to those, and deal with his attitude to them, in a few moments.
The reason given by the minister for this increase in interest rates is that it is necessary in order to attract additional funds into National Housing Act loans. He has said that the private lenders have refused to lend any further under the old rate, that sources of capital have dried up, and that the increase in the rate will re-attract them into the housing field. I hope the minister will tell us how this is going to happen and on what basis he arrived at this decision because we know that there is only so much investment money available today.
People who have arranged private mortgages have paid up to 8J per cent and 8J per cent interest. Industrial sections of the economy are paying 10 per cent interest, and the commercial sections are paying almost anything that is demanded of them. The minister takes the position that we are living in a free enterprise economy, and under that system investors will place their money where they receive the greatest return. If that be so, it is hard for me to understand how they will be attracted into the N.H.A. area where administration costs are greater, and where net returns are lower than on the type of loan.

November 24, 1966
Supply-Finance
The only other thing I wish to say, as a general observation, is that the government will never be able to solve all the problems in respect of housing unless it is prepared to create a separate ministry of housing and urban affairs and to delegate to it a full-time minister. I am not criticizing the present minister because he has had more than his share of labour troubles this year. I am sure it is on very rare occasions that he has a chance to sit back and think seriously about the whole housing crisis which exists in this country, and rarely that he can devote his energy and initiative to this field. This seems to be necessary if we are to even hope to find a solution.
I am sure that even with the appointment of a minister to a department of housing and urban affairs there will be no easy solution to this problem because of the jurisdictional matters involved. In this regard I quarrel with the minister who said in a Vancouver speech that he was opposed to the creation of such a ministry. He indicated that there are other ministries which should receive priority in their creation. What more important area could there be than housing which affects every Canadian from the cradle to the grave, which influences his evironment and has such a profound effect upon all his activities? What more important area could there be to justify the appointment of a full-time minister?
I know there is a constitutional problem which exists and which has always existed. When I was in the Ontario house I was told nothing could be done because of the federal problem. I am told in this house that nothing can be done because of a provincial problem. A constitutional game of hide and seek has been taking place.
When one reads the representations that have been made to the government, he realizes that our provinces and municipalities are desperate about this whole area of housing. They are crying out for leadership, direction and help and if this is not to come from Ottawa from where will it come? If initiative does not come from us now, when will there ever be initiative taken in this whole field?
Our whole approach today has been unproductive and without real response. As a result, the majority of Canadians are still not receiving the aid and direction they need. If we do not have a minister who is spending his full time in meeting with provinces, and through them with municipalities, to organize the conferences which are required, who is going to lead the way? We should have a minister travelling across the country to fight against

the maze of outdated building codes, stupid building regulations and prejudices among our local councils about public housing.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

Is the hon. member seriously suggesting that a federal minister should go into the different provinces and suggest to the municipalities that they should rewrite their laws, and that this minister should get into arguments with the municipalities about provincial laws when they are the responsibilities or as some say the creatures of provincial governments? Should a federal minister project himself into such a situation?

I am not suggesting that at all. I am suggesting that a federal minister should be prepared to go to the provinces and to organize conferences within those provinces, just as the minister has done in the past year, but in a very limited way. I think he took a very important step. I was glad to see that he accepted our suggestion because it has been productive of results. All I suggest is that a minister should lead the way and meet with provinces in an attempt to iron out these jurisdictional problems. I do not suggest they will easily or quickly be solved, but if we do not start now these problems will become worse. All these inbuilt rigidities will become more magnified in the future, making the solution of our housing problems more difficult.
As a first step we must have a minister and a department. The second thing we require, as is pointed out in the economic council's report, is the provision of more mortgage money at low enough rates to enable people to afford to buy houses. This does not involve throwing the whole problem of mortgage money on the private investment market, because that has not worked in the past and there is no indication it will work in the future. This again is an area where social and political decisions are needed in addition to the operation of the market place. This is again an area in which the government must lead and accept the responsibility for the general welfare of the public. This will again involve a complete reversal of the thinking that has taken place here in Ottawa. It will require the acceptance of the social responsi-bTty which rests upon the government in more and more areas of this kind.
As I say, conventional lenders cannot hope to supply the demand. We must be producing over 200,000 units per year by 1970, and that
November 24, 1966



is not far off, if we are to meet the targets set by the economic council. We are now a long way below that and the way we are going there is little possibility that we will really catch up. There must be a constant source of funds rather than the turning off and on of an economic tap, as it seems to me we have been doing in the past.
I have already alluded to the third thing required. We must have an enormous general planning program. This is not an original suggestion but was recognized by Mr. Deutsch in the report of the economic council. He suggested the whole problem has resulted from the failure of both levels of government to sit down together and plan some orderly development in the field of house construction generally. He suggested very strongly that these meetings should take place, that there should be conferences each fall and that a great deal more information should be collected as a result of conferences and discussions between all levels of government.
As a fourth step, we must expand enormously the activities of our co-operatives in public housing. We have just about reached the limit in many ways in the private sector, but the whole area of co-operative housing opens up tremendous possibilities in this country. In this way, perhaps we could make it possible for people collectively to build homes which they could afford to live in and purchase.
Our record in public housing is a disgrace. We have never really mastered the whole business of promoting public housing in this country, yet by the minister's own standards nobody earning under $5,000 per year can afford to buy a house in this country. These people will have to be housed in some way through public housing. Right now in Toronto we could place 25,000 people in public housing if we had the accommodation available. That is how desperate the situation has become. If you could see the chicken-coops and dog kennels, almost, in which Canadians are living in some of our large cities you might appreciate the gravity of the situation.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
We have never really got into the whole area of public housing. Again, leadership in this field must come from the central government; nobody else can give it. If the government does not give leadership, I do not think anybody will. Finally, Mr. Chairman, we have to launch a major assault on the whole area of urban development. There is some movement in this direction, but it is totally inadequate.
Supply-Finance
Even the minister has admitted this in his various speeches. We have a long, long way to go in this respect. This is an area in which you are fighting all kinds of local problems and prejudices.
And local landlords.

I agree; you are also fighting local landlords. Name it, and we have it; the whole gamut is there presenting a bulwark against any sort of social progress in this field. The minister, in his speeches, has indicated his awareness of this fact. Housing has been kicked around in Ottawa from department to department, and we have never had a really sustained program laid out by a minister.
These are some short-run solutions which seem to me to stand some chance of dealing adequately with the housing problem in Canada. We have not even touched upon the long-run solutions, of course. I can remember speaking in 1963, I think it was, on the same subject and suggesting to the minister that Canada faces problems of urbanization that stagger one's imagination; that as we move in the direction of urbanization, fantastic problems will be created for the urban dweller. There will be problems in the fields of transportation and communication. The whole problem of the urbanization of this country is falling upon us. I can find nothing that indicates that we have any idea of these long-run implications or what the long-run solutions may be. At that time we suggested to the minister that this was one area where a royal commission would be of use. I do not usually favour them; they are not always very successful. But it seems to me that in an area of gathering statistics and trend production a royal commission could be of great value. It could lay out for us-
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member not agree that this is a field in which the Economic Council, in view of their recommendations, might undertake the study?

I do not think so, because when the council appeared before us today they indicated that the informationgathering facilities in Canada are so poor they have virtually no really reliable statistics. An enormous change would have to be made in this type of statistical gathering before it would be reliable. The chairman was very honest and frank. He went right down the list and showed us the many areas in which no reliable statistics are available.

November 24, 1966
Supply-Finance
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I do not think the economic council could be properly used in this respect. It seems to me they will have their hands full in the next few years trying to gather the right kind of information on which to make projections in the field of investment, manpower, employment, trade, exports and those other matters which must be considered if we are to make any sort of adequate goals for the economy. I still think the royal commission would be a good idea. But if the minister can set up some investigating body under the council, I do not really care, as long as something is done now to find out what urbanization will do to Canada. If we wait, as we have waited with regard to housing, and just deal with it one a year-to-year crisis basis, many people of this country will curse us in the future.
Half the troubles in our big urban centres today have been caused by the fact we have never really planned ahead and tried to figure out these problems. We have never studied where we are going in this field and what we will need; therefore duplication and wastage of money can be found all over the place. If we do not do something to solve these problems, I think we will be cursed by later generations. There is also a committee of the house that might do some useful work in this area. To my knowledge, the housing committee has never met. There is no reason why some of this material should not be referred to that committee and useful studies undertaken by it. But the committee has not been convened, and nothing has been referred to it.
Those are the few remarks I wanted to make on behalf of the New Democratic Party. We do not think this change in the interest rate is justified or warranted. We think it will create hardship for our people. We do not think it will provide the flow of funds required, and even if it does bring in the money high priced houses will be built that the vast majority of people cannot afford anyway. As has been said, the N.H.A. is socialism for the rich and free enterprise for the poor. That is all that will be accomplished, even if you get the flow of money into the housing field. In the final analysis, the success or failure of the whole question of housing will devolve, I think, on the minister.
I repeat what I said three years ago, that the minister has an opportunity that most people in this house would envy. With sufficient energy, initiative, intelligence and resourcefulness, he has it in his power to start the process that will change the whole face of

this country. He has it within his power to regenerate our cities, to house our people adequately, to look after the elderly, to prepare for the growing families, to take care of our small towns which need rehabilitation, and to take care of the farm housing problem which exists. All this lies within his power if he has the initiative and courage to undertake it. This has not happened to date. I am not being unduly critical because the minister, as I said, has just too much to do. But perhaps now that he has all the strikes settled and all the labour problems out of the way, he can deal with this serious housing problem. I see that the minister raises his fingers, indicating that he has two labour problems to settle. Well, perhaps by Christmas the minister will have those problems out of the way, and for 1967 as his centennial project he might consider initiating a genuinely effective, progressive housing policy for Canada.
[DOT] (6.40 D.m.)

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have nothing much to add to the speech made by my hon. friend.
Of course, I think as always that the main deficiency of his speech is a lack of realism. For approximately half an hour, he dealt briefly with socialism, the housing problem, but mostly with urban development. If we want Canada to be a united country, we must realize that there is a constitution. I do not want to pass for a constitution maniac, but after seeing the federal government concern itself repeatedly with problems that are none of its business, such as urban development in Canada which comes under provincial jurisdiction, unnecessary conflicts are created. Federal members may have their own opinion about the problems of urban development, but even though they wished to solve them, they have no jurisdiction to do so. Why take up hours and hours to try and solve those problems in this house? We shall not succeed in solving them, and if we try, we shall only cause unnecessary trouble once again. Let each one stay in its field. We have enough problems to settle at the federal level; we should leave provincial problems in the hands of provincial authorities. I believe that is the only way to administer the country properly.
But I would rather deal with the rate of interest announced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) the other evening. I think that we should approach that problem realistically. Many will perhaps feel that the per cent
November 24, 1966

rate of interest is exaggerated. But the present circumstances must be taken into account. When we consider that the rate of interest of the C.M.H.C. is 6f per cent and that the province of Quebec has to pay more than 6J per cent on its bonds, well, it is unrealistic to want to borrow money for private houses at a lower rate than the governments must pay themselves for their own financial needs.
The interest rate on C.M.H.C. loans for urban renewal projects, low-cost housing, university students' residences, sewage systems, etc., varies every three months according to a formula included in the bill and according to a differential of J of 1 per cent more than the borrowing rate of the government.
As far as the present problem is concerned, if the general rate of interest of the C.M.H.C. does not change, along with the other interest rates of the corporation, then we develop a policy detrimental to the financing of public institutions, such as low-cost housing, university students' residences, etc. The minister responsible for the C.M.H.C. had no alternative but to change the rate of interest and set it at a more realistic rate.
Why set that rate? Because, at the present time, there is not a single private institution which is interested in lending money under the National Housing Act. Why? Because the rate of 6i per cent is not adjusted to the present interest rate. One knows very well that there are people who want to build houses and who now get loans at 8 and 8J per cent from financial institutions; consequently, why should those companies lend money at 6J per cent when they can get 8 per cent? Of course, the difference of 1| or 1J per cent was enough to cover the greater risk.
But if the interest rate is raised to 7J, then the private institutions might be interested in lending money under the National Housing Act. And those who are now getting loans at 8 per cent will get them at 7i per cent. Thus, we are helping those who want to build their own homes get lower interest rates. It may be too much at 7J per cent but, as mentioned earlier by the hon. member for York North (Mr. Addison), in those countries which are so dear to our friends of the New Democratic Party, in Sweden for instance, the interest rate on housing is higher than in Canada, and that country is supposed to be an earthly paradise. We know also that the rate in England and in France is much higher than in Canada. Of course, one must live with the times. The
Supply-Finance
interest rates are high because the international economy is forever expanding and the demand in all sectors is sustained. The demand being so heavy, the interest rate increases because there are less and less funds. To be practical, solutions must be found to help housing, and this is one of the solutions found by the minister, because it is said the present government is doing nothing to help housing.
In 1965, this government loaned directly, under the National Housing Act, $435 million, which is an unprecedented amount since the establishment of the corporation. As a matter of fact, from the time we came to power in 1963 until now, no previous administration has made more funds available to the C.M.H.C. than the present government.
One can say we are making a real effort. Maybe we could do more, but we must keep in mind the limits of the physical possibilities on the government; the borrowing capacity of any administration cannot be burdened indefinitely. I think we have, in the province of Quebec, a government which realizes that one cannot borrow without any limits. The problem is obvious enough now, what with the difficulties experienced at the moment by the province of Quebec in finding lenders on all the international money markets.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think a certain flexibility had to be introduced in this legislation. Since there was some flexibility in interest rates of loans for urban renewal of low-rental housing, student residences and sewage systems, the minister wanted to introduce the same flexibility here. Because of the present high interest rate in Canada, the interest rate for construction work will be 7i per cent, but if the money market becomes easier in the following months through the flexibility which the minister wanted to introduce in the legislation, then the interest rate will diminish. There are immediate advantages to be derived from this measure: many Canadians, I am sure, will be able tomorrow to get loans from private institutions at 7J per cent because of the change made by the minister. If the minister had not made this change, the same people who now want to build houses would have to pay 8, 8J or even 8J per cent interest on a first mortgage.
Therefore, I believe that, in introducing this legislation, the minister took a step which will help many Canadians to build a house more cheaply than they now can. If the 7J per cent rate seems rather high, in my opinion 7J per

November 24, 1966
Supply-Finance
cent is better than 8]- per cent, and I must support the minister in this initiative.

Mr. Chairman, when the minister made the announcement on Tuesday-evening that the interest rate for national housing was to be raised, my colleague the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke voiced the concern that we in this group share over a course that we believe will have nothing but detrimental effects upon our society as a whole. We cannot understand how the increasing of the interest rate for residential construction will be of benefit except perhaps, as has been pointed out, to some of those in the higher income brackets who will be able to go ahead and construct homes that only they are able to acquire. It means, as was pointed out in the memorandum from the Canadian Labour Congress, that those who are in the lower income brackets will have to be satisfied with the cast-offs of those who are in a better financial position.
They will be unable to afford homes at all.

That is right. Under the circumstances, it is difficult to understand just how they will be able to secure any type of accommodation.
The reason the minister gave for this increase in the interest rate was that it was to encourage or attract investment capital for residential construction. The question has been raised just how this will happen. I do not believe that this step will result in the realization of the stated objective; but as I have pointed out we do know that it will create a very unhappy situation for prospective homeowners.
An article appearing in today's Gazette in the colunm "Your Business" by John Meyer carries the heading "New N.H.A. rate right step taken much too late". I do not agree that it is a right step, but I should like to read part of the second paragraph so as to raise the question whether the step taken by the government is actually going to improve the supply of capital for residential construction:
The increase in the rate from 62 to 72 per cent is not going to attract much in the way of new funds, certainly not enough to make an appreciable difference in the number of starts during the first half. Conventional mortgage rates are 8 per cent or higher; with a spread of 2 point or more, N.H.A. mortgages simply aren't that competitive.
So, this writer raises the question whether this step will help reach the objective outlined by the minister.

In speaking on the second reading of the housing act amendments bill I made some general observations, which I do not intend to repeat at this time. Canada's housing requirements have been referred to on a great number of occasions. I think the hon. member for Danforth is quite right when he says that we must look upon housing as something that is absolutely essential to the social structure of our nation. It cannot be looked upon just as a matter of economics. We must consider the fact that if we are to promote that type of society and family life which we believe will be effective in the development and maintenance of our national life, housing is absolutely essential.
[DOT] (6.50 p.m.)
We know that housing requirements will have to meet the needs of increased numbers of immigrants if the government's plans work out. A great many homes are required to meet the needs of new family formations. We cannot, therefore, look with any degree of equanimity at a situation that allows us to lag so far behind in meeting essential housing needs.
Several factors militate against the housing situation and the availability of housing for our people. The high cost of housing now pretty well leaves the vast majority of Canadians out in the cold. They have no possibility of investing in a home under the present circumstances. Many people must be satisfied with inferior types of housing, left by some of those who have moved higher in the scale. High interest rates are another hurdle our people have been fighting to overcome. Now, we find that the people have to face an even higher interest rate which will militate against any possibility of their achieving homes of their own.
Tight money, the labour shortage and all these other things have been referred to, and they all have a detrimental effect on housing. We heard a great deal a couple of years ago about the desirability of home ownership, and we talked about the possibility of every person in Canada being able to acquire his own home, to maintain dignity and give a sense of security. We felt that this was good for this great and growing nation. We talked in glowing terms of the time when all people would be able to own and occupy their own homes.
Immediately thereafter the government engaged in actions that worked to the opposite effect, making it practically impossible for the people of Canada to realize their objectives of home ownership. I suggest that instead of the
November 24, 1966

government moving towards increased interest rates, tightening money and so on, it should be engaged in a program that would enable our people to obtain and enjoy their own homes, to be able to bring up their families in decency as they have every right to do.
The government imposed the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, and this followed immediately after that talk of the desirability of people owning their own homes. The government moved toward withdrawing the exemption of sales tax on building materials. It was very difficult for the people of Canada to understand why the government moved in that direction, and it was difficult for them to understand how the government could reconcile its action with the talk that everybody should own his own home.
I think the request is properly in order. It is made by the National House Builders Association. The association suggests, in a document I hold that:
The rebating of the 11 per cent sales tax on residential building materials could prove most effective.
The minister is aware of the representations which have been made about this matter. The government refused to yield and still refuses. Now, it has increased the interest rate making it almost impossible for most Canadians to own their own homes.
There was also a grant program that enabled people to construct their own homes and to receive a rebate of $500. That has gone by the board. I do not know why. Perhaps it was too effective, so the government decided to withdraw from that program. Here again, the government action militates against those objectives it was encouraging in Canada. It is hard to reconcile the two positions of the government. There are those words uttered by the Prime Minister about the desirability of extending the house building program and making funds available for home purchases, and the present government announcement. It is difficult to reconcile the two.
A suggestion by the National House Builders Association is for the introduction of legislation to amend the Income Tax Act to allow home owners to deduct from their taxable incomes payments of taxes and mortgage interest. This would have a beneficial effect. It is said that the administrative problems might be so great as to prevent the implementation of such a thing, but I do not believe that. Such an amendment ought to be brought in and implemented.
23033-653J
Supply-Finance
In addition to that, we ought to consider the recommendation this afternoon of the hon. member for York North that consideration be given to allowing depreciation on residential housing. After all, consideration is given to depreciation with respect to commercial property. Residential housing ought to be considered in the same way as commercial property. Here again, though the people are asked to accept an added burden, they would feel they were benefiting, and that they were not suffering too greatly by government action.
Instead of hiking the interest rate, the government should provide additional capital at much lower rates to continue the housing program and to help our people.
Hear, hear.

On second reading of the banking legislation I suggested that to release the pressure on private investment capital the government, through the Bank of Canada, ought to make social capital available for schools, hospitals and things like that. The government should make available, through a municipal development bank or some agency of the Bank of Canada, capital to meet those needs thereby taking the pressure off the available private capital which would then be diverted to housing.
I want once again to state, as strongly as I can, our objection to the procedure that the government is taking in this particular area, because it will drastically affect the welfare of our people in all walks of life from coast to coast.

I had hoped to speak during the committee stage on Bill No. C-241 but unfortunately I could not. I am grateful for th's opportunity, in the estimates of the Minister of Finance, to say a few words about housing.
Again I want to commend the minister for the amendments, by way of Bill No. C-241, to provide N.H.A. loans for older homes. Of course, these loans have been promised since 1943. I am glad that belatedly this promise has been fulfilled. I again urge the minister not to set the amount of loans too low, because if loans go up to $10,000 only-as has been quoted-they will not have the effect of rehabilitating those houses most in need of rehabilitation. In other words, if a loan is for $10,000, and of that $2,000 has to be used for improvements, that loan will not rehabilitate the type of house most capable of being rehabilitated. I suggest that a figure of $14,000 or $15,000 would be more reasonable.

November 24. 1966
Supply-Finance
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
I wanted to say to the minister that by the answers he had given in the house I knew he was considering raising the interest rates. I wish to advance at least one reason why I believe it would be better to make more money available through direct loans than to increase the interest rate.
Would the hon. member permit a question? If the government keeps borrowing, does he not think the government's rates for such borrowing will also go up?

Yes, indeed. But looking at this from the point of view of the individual I believe it is good for a young couple to own their home. I am thinking particularly of those in the lower income brackets. Housing is not entirely a matter of finance. There is a social aspect involved.
Hear, hear.

I believe that the federal government has a responsibility for showing initiative. Responsibility also rests with provincial governments and the municipalities. But the initiative lies with the federal government and the action which the government has now taken will, I believe, make it still more difficult for those who most need housing to raise the money they require. Admittedly the government's action will make more money available. That is obvious, I think. As to the provision for making loans available in respect of existing houses, that is a major step in the right direction and I commend the government on having taken it.
One reason the minister should have made more money available by means of direct loans arises out of the condition created by the press release which C.M.H.C. issued on July 27 and bulletin No. 181 of July 29. I have read these documents repeatedly. I agree that if one reads them very carefully one will see there is an out inasmuch as they say "subject to moneys being available". But I wish to tell the hon. gentleman very sincerely that I have spoken to many contractors in my own area and to the president of the Victoria Home Builders Association, and I know that a general impression was created among the builders, particularly among the smaller ones, that the whole intent of this press release and bulletin was to announce that funds would be available for the winter period.
The result was that many small contractors did not apply for funds before August 1 because the bulletin gave the impression that they had until the end of September in which

to make application, during which period direct loans would be made available to speculative builders as a means of increasing construction in the winter. This was the impression created, particularly in view of the fact that the $500 winter construction bonus was to be removed. I am not blaming the manager of the local C.M.H.C. branch office, because he had been urging all contractors to make their applications early. As it was, many of those who put in their applications early enough were given direct loans-nine, in one case, and so on. I agree that now the interest rate has been raised a greater amount of conventional money will be available, but the builders who put in their applications early and received direct loans will nevertheless be in an unfair competitive position compared with those who did not get their applications in before August 1.
As to the whole question of the government's attitude toward housing, I have indicated that I believe there is a social aspect involved. A man earning $8,000 or $10,000 a year can normally finance a home whether the interest rate is 7j>- per cent or 8 per cent. But people earning lower incomes and elderly people find themselves in a very different situation. I am sure the minister has read the report of the Senate committee on aging. According to that report there are some 300,000 elderly families and elderly single people who are in need of housing. The type of financing we are talking about this evening cannot help them in any way. According to the minister's own report, fewer than 1,700 units have been provided by way of public housing.

I would not want any such impression to be left on the record. In the province of Ontario alone indications are that there will be as much public housing built or started in 1966 as was built in approximately half the last decade, as much in one year as in five years in one province.

I was speaking of actual starts. I am sure that what the minister said is correct. The minister spoke of anticipated buildng. But that does not mean very much since according to the Senate committee report only 13,000 rental units have been provided since 1939 of which only 167 were earmarked for old people. Even if this record were increased fivefold it would not touch the need. The annual report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation says that according to statistical evidence the housing need among old people in Canada is large and widespread.
November 24, 1966

I have been talking about the immediate demand for housing on the part of elderly-people. The next group I wish to consider consists of people earning less than $5,000 a year. I am sure the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials was a wrong tax, one of the worst that could have been imposed. Granted, the government needed money but surely there was a better means of obtaining revenue than by imposing a tax on building materials. One of the largest house builders in my area told me that the effect of this sales tax was something like $1,000 per house. I understand that in the Toronto area the cost of the average house has increased by 26 per cent in the last 18 months. The first increase this year was on January 10, a 15 per cent increase in the cost of building. This puts even farther out of the reach of the low income family, the family which in my opinion needs it most, any prospect of decent housing.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
I can do no better, Mr. Chairman, than to quote from today's Ottawa Citizen, a paper that has not been too hostile to the Liberal party, an editorial headed, "Try Again, Mr. Nicholson." It reads in part:
Labour Minister Nicholson, in announcing higher interest rates on National Housing Act loans late Tuesday evening, has just added to the pressures that are making the ownership of new homes increasingly out of the range of people in middle income brackets.
The editorial says "middle", and I would say even farther out of the reach of the low income bracket people. I continue reading from the editorial:
-where Mr. Nicholson has so far erred is in insisting that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation's participation in the direct loan field has to be limited to a small proportion of the total of insured loans offered by N.H.A. Throughout the year Mr. Nicholson has been insisting home builders should be seeking their funds on the regular money markets. The effect has been that the government's direct loans for residential construction have been limited to 31,500 units, the same as last year, in a period when government policies have dried up funds from investment houses.
I conclude with this quotation from the last paragraph of the editorial:
The errors of our ways are pointed out in detail in the Economic Council report. It is up to the government now to come up with some long-range solutions.
I believe the minister to be sincere and conscientious. I know he has been busy with all kinds of problems and is involved with two major ones at the moment, but I urge him to look at this matter not from the point of view of straight finance but from the point of view of the social impact of housing in a country
Supply-Finance
such as Canada. I have always believed that if a couple own their own home they own a piece of Canada. They are more likely to be responsible citizens who take an interest, first of all, in local affairs and then go from there to provincial affairs, then to national affairs and eventually international affairs.
I do not say that when our government was in power it was perfect in any way or that it did all those things which it should have done. But I do say that the statistics are clear as to the growing number of families needing homes. This problem is going to become aggravated. The action of the government in raising interest rates will provide some additional money but it puts home ownership farther out of the reach of the people who need housing most. I urge the minister to make more direct funds available for prospective home owners, even at the increased interest rate if that is necessary.
I think the statistics provided by C.M.H.C.. are probably better in many respects than those provided by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. We have all the necessary information available. We should use it to provide a long-term plan, keeping in mind the social aspects of housing in a country like Canada.
