speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Ville-neuve can be quite sure that the Chair will recognize him but at the moment the Chair recognizes the hon. member for Verdun.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I do not think we can let that remark pass. All of us in the chamber are aware of your fairness and impartiality, and I think the record should show that nobody in the Creditiste group stood and indicated a desire to speak prior to the appearance in the chamber of the leader of the party just a short time ago.

It is the custom in the house when we start debating a question that each party has the opportunity to speak. We did not attempt to use our opportunity at the start but I want to use it now, and I think I was fair in saying what I just said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I think the hon. member for Villeneuve should recognize that when this discussion first began an effort was made by the Chair to recognize each party in turn, as is usually done. Nobody from his party rose at that particular time. The hon. member for Fraser Valley spoke following that, and the Chair now recognizes the hon. member for Verdun.
That is all right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I shall keep my remarks brief and to the point, following the trend of the very objective discussion we have had so far and the very encouraging suggestions that have been made. I find myself practically in complete agreement with the hon. member for Danforth and other speakers-
You were not the other night.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I said practically. It is just a matter of degree, because I think the theme running through most of the speeches so far is that there is no member of the House of Commons who believes there should be any Canadian without decent housing, particularly in a country that prides itself on its affluent society and the fact that it is one of the richest nations in the world.
Where I may differ a little with some hon. members is on the matter of priorities, and I wish to make my point in my own rather odd manner. I should like to review briefly the

history of housing in Canada and the evolution of C.M.H.C. and the National Housing Act. 1 wish to review the situation in 1946 when C.M.H.C. in essence, took over the various federal departments that existed then looking after housing during the war.
All of us who are old enough to recall 1946 will remember it was the year when thousands of members of the armed forces were returning to Canada, anxious to forget the war years and particularly anxious to enter what they called civvy street, to attend universities, to resume their marriages or to get married. This created a particular type of housing problem, one that was very adequately met by legislation and amendments to the National Housing Act that were introduced to help alleviate the problem.
I can recall 1946 very vividly from personal experience. I bought a home that year under the provisions of the National Housing Act. At that time land in my riding, because it is on the island of Montreal, was fairly expensive but I and many other people were able to obtain a good, self-contained dwelling on a lot 50 feet by 100 feet for $5,000. At one time such dwellings could be obtained for $4,800 but by the time I, like other timid people, took the plunge they were selling around $5,000. I am using round figures for simplification's sake.
* (7:20 p.m.)
This meant that with a mortgage spread over 20 years, available from a life insurance company and endorsed by the government, the principal cost me $20 a month. The interest, at the prevailing rate at the time of 4J per cent, came to another $15 a month and municipal taxes $25 a month, making a total of $60 a month. For $60 a month I was able to fit in the price picture mentioned by the hon. member who just sat down. For $60 a month and a rather modest down payment I could own my own home, garden and the rest of it. This is very realistic. This experience, of course was repeated across the nation. But hon. members know the economic changes we went through. Land became scarce, particularly in the centre of cities and even on the immediate perimeter, and people were forced out to suburbia, as we call it, in order to take advantage of lower land costs. Municipalities then began introducing stricter building codes which added to the cost. The people who moved out to these areas found that what they had saved on land they were losing in transportation costs and so on.
November 24, 1966



Twenty years later the situation has evolved into one where the same type of person is faced with the fact that if he wants similar accommodation to that which I had he must assume a mortgage in the amount of $15,000. In an effort to verify this fact I inquired today at Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and was advised that on the average the amount of an N.H.A. mortgage is $15,000 per home. With the increase in the interest rate this will mean an increase of $4.50 a month in the payment. The point I am trying to make is that even at a 2 per cent interest rate, with the tremendous increase in municipal and school taxes the average couple in my area would be expected to meet a monthly payment of close to $175. These are the facts, even figuring it at 2 per cent, let alone at 7-| per cent.
Like the hon. member for Danforth and others I am vitally concerned about the plight of the senior citizens and those people whom we used to call the poor. The average income in Canada is around $6,000. A man earning $6,000 cannot afford a $15,000 mortgage today. This is what we should understand. The increase in the interest rate, which will generate more money, no doubt will stimulate housing starts in the category of $15,000 mortgages, but I couldn't give a damn, if I may use that expression in the House of Commons, for the people who need that type of a home. I am concerned about those who are earning $4,800, $5,000 or $6,000, as well as the older people who go into convalescent homes and other fire traps where they are left to die. The Eskimos were more kind to their senior citizens when they left them on an ice floe. These are the people in whom I am interested. The rate of interest in respect of loans available to help this group of people has not been increased. I think this is important.
In all fairness to the minister I think it should be re-emphasized that the rate of interest has not been increased in respect of loans to municipalities and through provincial housing authorities under section 16A of the National Housing Act which are designed to provide homes for the senior citizens of Canada. This is done through municipal authorities or by non-profit organizations, service clubs and other media with which I and everyone in this house is familiar. Many of us who have participated in this debate because of our deep concern for the plight of the people and the obvious necessity for a new or expanded policy in respect of urban renewal have forgotten the fact that the increase in the interest rate will work a hardship on persons who can
Supply-Finance
afford a $15,000 mortgage. The amount of the average mortgage under the National Housing Act is $15,000. I feel that if a young man can afford a $15,000 mortgage he can also afford $4.50 more a month in interest. He is not concerned about the interest rate but rather with the fact that money is not available at all. He is quite willing to pay 10 per cent if he can find the money.
These are accurate figures, and this brings me back to the point made by the hon. member for Danforth and others. What is the federal policy in respect of providing housing for those people in Canada who need it? Let us define who these people are. I will shorten my remarks. I had intended to quote some statistics, but I know that at least two ministers wish to participate in this debate. I think we must be blunt and say to the average married couple who are 22 or 23 years of age that it is not in their best interests to assume a $15,000 mortgage particularly when they have no children or perhaps only one or two. What we need and need badly in this country are housing projects in which the average young couple just starting out in the labour force can rent an adequate home. I am not speaking of projects such as we had 10 or 15 years ago which became slums. I have in mind projects which will have some dignity and will have recreational areas and schools close by. This is what we need. I think too the government and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation must investigate the new concept of land leasing.
I might mention a good example of a land leasing operation in my area. A project is being developed on precisely these terms. A person can buy a home and rent the land for 99 years. As usual this type of imaginative project is being financed and sponsored by United States interests and with United States capital. An effort was made over a period of ten years or more to find the capital in Canada to develop this project and because it was unsuccessful United States interests were finally attracted to the project.
I know there are many others who wish to speak and I will be brief. I should like to say, however, that we just cannot hide behind the B.N.A. Act. We must give direction and I think we are giving direction. I refer to the latest bulletin issued by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I am sure that everyone who has participated in this debate must have had a look at it. Normally Quebec looks upon

November 24, 1966
Supply-Finance
this type of financial assistance which is available to municipalities with a degree of suspicion. However, I note, for instance, that a loan of $350,000 was advanced to the Y.W.C.A. for the construction of a hostel which will have 112 beds. This is just a random example.
[DOT] (7.30 p.m.)
There are other examples to be noted. For example, a loan was provided to the city of Montreal that ran into millions of dollars to provide housing for those people who really need it rather than for young people who can afford a $15,000 mortgage. I am concerned about the man who makes $92 a week and goes to work with a lunch pail under his arm. He wants to rent a decent flat at a fair rental, preferably in the heart of the city near recreational facilities and his church. This is the challenge which faces Canadians, but it is not a challenge to be faced exclusively by the federal government.
Many months ago I mentioned my own community as an example of communities that have not assumed their moral responsibility to their senior citizens. Cities and towns should develop their own housing projects. I had suggested this so often in debate that someone wrote me a letter pointing out that I was not only a member of parliament but a citizen of a community and asked me what I had done about the situation. This bothered me for several reasons and I did something about it. I went to the community and appeared before the local council and acquainted them with what is available in the way of money. This community has now reached an agreement on a project and has been informally assured by the province that it will approve the project. In the city of Verdun we are now building a community project for our senior citizens which should accommodate over 100 couples. At the same time the local Lions Club in conjunction with the city, which is going to either give them the land, lease it or lend it to them for 100 years, intends to build a project which will accommodate 35 or 40 individuals.
The whole point I am trying to make is that the federal government is not shirking its responsibilities in this important area. There are millions of dollars available to communities which get off their fannies and do something about this problem instead of coming here whining to the federal government or to members of parliament. The citizens of the communities should be getting after their reeves or aldermen and asking them what they are doing for the $400 a month or so they
[Mr. Mackasey.l
are receiving. In other words, social groups and church groups should re-examine their consciences and get after their civic representatives to do something and take advantage of federal legislation. No matter how much we rant and rave about the situation we can do nothing under the B.N.A. Act but make money available and hope the communities will take advantage of it.
Let me put on record one or two examples of what took place in September, a month which was full of activity in public housing. Some communities across Canada are doing things in conjunction with the federal government to solve their housing problems. I heard someone suggest that the federal government advance money for research before a project is started. We do just that, Lachute, Quebec, received in September, $14,000 to pay for research to determine exactly what its need is. As the hon. member for Danforth suggested, this type of research could be done through a royal commission, but funds are available to communities right now.
Let me point out to members the scale on which these funds are available to municipalities across the country. After all, the communities should know their needs best and it is up to the civic leaders elected to do something about the situation. Longueuil received $15,000, Newmarket, Ontario, received $6,900, and Shaunavon, Saskatchewan, received $7,500.
This document also indicates that $1,688,082 was authorized by the federal government during the month for low rental projects comprising 82 self-contained housing units and hostel accommodation for 250 persons. It then gives details of loans approved under section 16A of the act, but I shall not read them all. Fort Qu'Appelle received $204,000; Gladstone, Manitoba, received $89,000; La Sarre, Quebec, received $291,000-these are round figures -Lundar, Manitoba, received $72,000; Ottawa received $277,000; Quebec city received $350,000; Regina, Saskatchewan, received $45,000, and Yorkton, Saskatchewan, received $357,000. I am more impressed by these figures and the projects for which these loans are being made than I am by complaints of young executives who are upset because of some unaccountable reason they cannot find the ways and means of assuming a $15,000 mortgage.
I agree with a great deal of what has been said today and the principles enunciated by hon. members. It is a shame that any Canadian should be living in a substandard
November 24, 1968

hovel, which is what too many of them are doing today. The fact still remains however, that we have a duty to establish priorities and stick by them. The last individual who needs assistance, as long as our senior citizens cannot find accommodation, is the one who can afford a $15,000 mortgage. I am worried about the individuals who earn $89, $100 or $110 per week and who can afford to rent a decent place in which to live but cannot because such housing is in short supply. I am sure the hon. member for Danforth and those of other parties who have spoken are also concerned about these people.
When members get up in this house and say that because we have allowed the interest rate to increase by half of one per cent, we are creating a tremendous hardship they are not being accurate. The increase will in effect mean an increased payment of $4.50 per month for those who have a $15,000 mortgage. I do not know of anyone who is in a better position to pay $4.50 per month than the individual who is earning $8,000 to $12,000 per year.
Before anyone, including myself, condemns the federal government, let us do a little soul-searching as individual citizens of communities. Let us ask the elected officials of those communities why they do not take advantage of the money made available by the federal government in order to wipe out slums and provide decent housing accommodation for the senior citizens. If there is anyone here today that should be doing some soul-searching in respect of this problem it is not the Minister of Labour nor the House of Commons; it is those individuals who run the communities across the country. They continually try to transfer their responsibilities to the shoulders of higher authorities.
We provide the money, the research and the know-how. We have regional offices all across the country. We can do nothing more under the B.N.A. Act but ask those communities to seize the initiative and take advantage of funds available to bring to their communities the type of housing they need.

Mr. Chairman, my first words are directed to the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) who is asking the municipalities and the communities of our country to take their responsibilities. I wish to tell him that he should start by bringing
Supply-Finance
some relief to the Canadian taxpayers, so that they may be able to pay their school and municipal taxes; then, the school boards or the communities will probably be able to allow these individuals to have some property or some assets.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. I have a high respect for the hon. member and I think in all sincerity he does not wish to misconstrue my remarks. I was referring to the areas where interest rates have not been increased. I was talking specifically about the funds available to communit;es within his riding for senior citizens' projects, low rental projects, slum clearance and improvements of this kind in the social area. This has nothing to do with school taxes or municipal taxes; it is a medium by which communities can borrow from the federal government 90 per cent of the money needed, with repayment over a greatly extended period of time.
[DOT] (7.40 p.m.)
I agree with the hon. member that the average community, particularly in my province, is paying through the nose for school taxes and the average home owner in small communities cannot afford this additional burden. This brings me back to my original argument, that young people between 20 and 25 years of age who are thinking of assuming a $15,000 mortgage should get the advice of someone they can trust, someone who can put the facts before them and point out to them that it is not always in their best interests to assume this kind of burden at that age.

I would ask the hon. member to join another political party so we can solve this problem, because there is no solution in what the government is proposing now.

Mr. Chairman, in my opinion, raising of the interest rate on loans from 6J per cent to 71 per cent, ostensibly to help small wage-earners, does not bring any solution to the problems with which we are now faced. And I am sorry that the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp) is not in the house at the present time. His parliamentary secretary (Mr. Chretien) is here but the minister himself is absent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I answer the question put by the hon. member? The money is raised either from the taxpayers or by borrowing on the market, just as we
November 24, 1966

would raise money for any other purpose. I can assure him that it costs the taxpayers their taxes or costs the government money to pay interest on the money the government has to borrow. It is not borrowed by the Canadian government without cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer to that question, Mr. Chairman, is also simple. This is a form of external aid. I am sure that my hon. friend would agree that Canada has a responsibility to help underprivileged countries of the world which do not enjoy the good fortune of Canada.
Hear, hear.

I enjoy the applause by hon. members of the Liberal party, but would the minister come with me to my own district or to the city of Montreal, the city of Quebec, or around Lake St. John or to the western part of Canada or to the maritime provinces, where I can show him just as much misery as exists in Bolivia, the Congo or anywhere else in the world?

I hear the hon. member for Saint-Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) say that it is not true. I will take the hon. member to his own city of Shawinigan and show him the misery which prevails in his own region.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I would rather live in
Shawinigan than in Bolivia.

Certainly, in view of the salary you are getting here, you are certainly better off living in Shawinigan than in Bolivia. However, the rest of the people in Shawinigan, the workers, the unemployed, and those who have to live on social allowances only are not much better off than those in Bolivia, the Congo or any other African country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is demagoguery.
Supply-Finance

Mr. Chairman, as I understand it, it is always demagogy when the time comes to help our own people. But when it is time to help others and assume our responsibilities, it is a different matter. I have no objection to helping other people who need assistance, but I object when the powers that be refuse to help first our own people who lack the necessities of life throughout the country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What about social security?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice-Lafleche talks to me about social security.
Just before coming in the house, I was reading a letter from my riding where there is no more hardship than in Shawinigan, Drummondville or Victoriaville, or in the riding of the Minister of Finance.
Let us take, for instance, the case of a mother with four children who only gets $125 a month and pays a monthly rent of $60. How can she manage with $65 a month to provide for herself and her children?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Could I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does he not realize that there are a great many people in the world whose annual income is not as large as the monthly income of those people in his constituency, who I am quite sure deserve more help and I hope will get it? But I do not think this is any excuse for our not helping the millions and millions of very poor people in the world who without our help are going to die.

Mr. Chairman, speaking with full knowledge of the facts, I wish to say that I visited Iran not so long ago, two months ago as a matter of fact, accompanied by some of my good friends from the Liberal party. We have seen poverty, even abject poverty. It is a fact. One evening, at the Canadian embassy, we met people from Canada, Canadian engineers teaching mechanical engineering to Iranians. One of the professors I met told me: I have been here for nine months. I have tried everything to drill technical know-how into Iranians; after nine months I have not succeeded in teaching one iota of what I have learned in Canada. And the Canadian government wants me to teach

November 24, 1966
Supply-Finance
them in two years what it took me six years to learn in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, we saw real poverty. I have seen it with my own eyes. For instance, I went, with my good friend, the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pilon), to the northern mountains of Teheran, towards the Caspian Sea, where we saw antiquated things, such as could be seen in ancient times: camel, mule and donkey caravans. We would have seen our Saviour Jesus Christ with the twelve apostles and we would probably not have been surprised, because their standard of living and their way of life have remained what they were 2,000 years ago. But that does not mean, Mr. Chairman, that we should neglect Canada or the Canadian people. I have no objection to doing everything we can to help those people. But let us stop imposing on Canadians as a whole more sacrifices to make them tenants instead of home owners. That is where I do not go along with the Minister of Finance.
The Minister of Finance is well aware of Canadian production. It is very well to rise and say: we should feed the poor of the world, we should help them; our own people on social or public assistance are better off than the working people in those countries.
It is all very well for them to sing us that song here and I sincerely believe that we have people getting social assistance benefits who live better than the working people in those countries. But if those people are unable to improve their financial system in a better way than Canada is improving its own, requiring all the time sacrifices from plain folks and allowing the people to get richer, the Creditistes are not going to accept that.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
The hon. Minister of Finance is aware of the situation. If our Canadian people do not have the standard of living they should enjoy and are entitled to, this is nothing to do with national production; it is a question of national revenue, a question of monetary policy, and until such a policy has been adjusted to conditions, production or physical possibilities we have in Canada, the Minister of Finance will spend his time introducing measures like this, namely increasing the interest rate from 6f to 7J per cent, so as to help plain folks to lose their property. The Minister of Finance knows that when a Canadian buys a $15,000 house, taking into account the interest rate that will be required as of now on and the reimbursement

period spread over 25, 30 or 35 years, that house will cost from $25,000 to $30,000.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance is very well aware that the house building problem and the housing problem, as regards everybody in this country, is not a problem of physical possibilities. All the unemployed living at present in Quebec, or elsewhere, could be hired to build good houses for the Canadian people, and in order to do this, it is not necessary, as pointed out earlier by the hon. member for Verdun, to resort to the British North America Act. It is not necessary to appeal to anybody, if the minister can or decides to assume his own responsibilities. Let the minister stop once and for all telling us that only two ways of getting money are available to the government when it needs it, namely taxes or loans. That is what the minister told us a while ago; Only two ways of securing funds are available to the government, loans or taxes, and I should like the minister to tell me-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I did not say that there are only two methods of raising money. I said we are employing only these methods. There is a third method that apparently the hon. member advocates, and that is inflation. That we are trying to avoid.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to hear the minister say that the third way is inflation.
For his information, I will tell the minister what I read in the Canada Year Book recently and told the members of the Canadian bankers association who were present at the meeting of the finance, trade and economic affairs committee tonight at eight o'clock. When the federal government issues bonds for $1 million-and the Minister of Finance knows this-our national institution, the Bank of Canada, buys one million dollars worth of federal bonds; this increases by as much the total reserves of the Canadian chartered banks and allows the latter to issue $12.5 million dollars of new credit and to lend money to the government. The minister knows this. Instead of issuing one million dollars worth of bonds, why does the minister not issue $12.5 million in credit without interest, instead of forcing the Canadian people to pay interest on fictitious credit issued by the Canadian chartered banks?
Does the minister wish to say anything else?
November 24. 1966

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is a short answer to that question. The method we are now following I think will have much more beneficial effects than the application of Social Credit principles which have not been adopted by any country in the world.

This is a fine reason, Mr. Chairman. For 2000 years now, the Bible has been preached throughout the whole world, and there are still people going to the devil every day. Will the fact that people are going to the devil every day keep preachers from going on with their preaching?
The minister points out the fact that there are no Creditistes or no Creditiste government anywhere in the world. Is this an answer? Does it mean that we cannot begin, here in Canada, giving an example to the whole world? With respect to peace, we all say, with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin): let us set an example for the world. But in the financial field, Mr. Chairman, if the Minister of Finance, (Mr. Sharp) and the present Liberal government decided to show the way to the world, not by printing money without restriction or without any consideration, but by implementing a monetary system corresponding exactly to the physical criteria, to our country's production, would this not set an example for other countries in the world to follow? Could we not finance by ourselves what we can develop here?
Mr. Chairman, why must we always go to the United States, for instance, or to Europe- but most of the time to the United States-to beg financial permission to build a trans-Canada highway, schools, hospitals, to develop our provinces and our municipalities? Why, if we are physically able to develop our own country, Canada, can we not create the credit or the currency corresponding to our own production?
And then, as Abraham Lincoln, one-time President of the United States said, our money would be as sound as our country would be, because, to the extent that the people, with the help of their government-naturally- with the help of their Minister of Finance, their economists, will build a country represented by an adequate monetary system, there will be security and freedom for each and everyone.
Mr. Chairman, my colleagues, members of the Ralliement Creditiste and myself object to
Supply-Finance
this increase in the rate of interest on residential housing projects. It does not solve the problem and, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) was saying yesterday, chartered banks will enter the conventional loan market. Eventually, they will come into this market and will be able to grant loans bearing interest at a much lower rate than 7J or 6] per cent, since their power to multiply money enables them to operate at costs ranging between 1J, If, or 2 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, when people apply for loans, why does the Minister of Labour or the Minister of Finance object? Why do they submit plans to increase the interest rate when those interests are at present the cause of inflation in Canada. And when the Minister of Finance told me laughing that there were three means to meet the financial needs of the country: in the first place, loans, second, taxes and third inflation, it is exactly the third means which the Minister of Finance now suggests that is inflation which makes the poor poorer and the rich richer.
Well, Mr. Chairman, we will side with the poor to fight the rich who want to continue their shameless exploitation of the common workers in Canada and in Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to participate in the debate on this most important subject of housing and what should be done to try to solve the problem. In participating I may say that my only wish is to try to put the subject into some reasonable or logical context.
I have listened with great interest and great satisfaction to the remarks of most members who have participated in the debate. The remarks on the whole have been constructive. Hon. members have shown a knowledge- perhaps I should also say a sympathy-with regard to this important problem and they have suggested various methods of solving it. Some hon. members have criticized the increase announced two days ago in the interest rate on most N.H.A. lending. That I will refer to later.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
More than one reference has been made in the course of the debate to the very marked decline in housing starts this year. As I have said more than once, starts this year will total approximately 130,000 units compared with 166,600 last year. Dwelling completions this year, however, have been much higher than

November 24, 1966
Supply-Finance
the number of starts; also there was an encouraging number of starts after the middle of August. This year we shall complete 155,000 houses, slightly more than the number of completions in the record years prior to 1965. These totals, I must say, compare with an increase in housing needs which may average close to 170,000 houses per annum for the next three years or so. Indeed, as mentioned by the hon. member for Danforth, it may well reach a level of 200,000 per annum in the early '70's.
The government recognizes that this disparity between housing production and housing needs cannot be allowed to continue. The Economic Council of Canada has pointed out in its recent report the necessity for early action and I entirely support the recommendations the council has made. The need is to find solutions to bring about the desired result. I might say that there is no single action which could be taken by this or any other government to bring those two figures into better balance. There must be an attack on several fronts and in this connection a few figures might be helpful in placing the matter in proper perspective.
Of the 130,000 housing units started in 1966, close to 50,000 units are being financed by the federal government under the National Housing Act. This is an increase of over 30 per cent over any other year in Canada's history. Another 60,000 units are being financed by conventional loans from the lending institutions, as against a total of 100,000 by them in previous years, a drop of 40 per cent this year. The remaining 20,000 or so units are being financed outside the institutional mortgage market by people who can afford to use their own money or borrow from the banks, or perhaps they sell one house and build another with the proceeds. But of the 50,000 units financed under N.H.A., nearly 35,000, approximately one-quarter of our total housing production in Canada in 1966, are being financed by direct loans through C.M.H.C.
This is a much higher proportion of government assistance to the housing program than at any time in Canada's history. This assistance has involved an expenditure of public funds through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation amounting to more than $600 million in one year. This, I might say, is well above the 1964 and 1965 record totals of $400 million and $500 million respectively. I might also mention that the increase has been even more marked in the field of assistance to
housing for low income groups and for the elderly. A record figure, $65 million, was spent in 1965 for such housing, but the total will be approximately $100 million in 1966 and there is every indication that in 1967 the figure will be considerably higher still.
In Ontario, the province has embarked on a program to build within two years approximately the same number of public housing units as were built in the whole of Canada in the previous decade and I am advised that the program is right on target. Ninety per cent of the money for that program is being provided on loan by the federal government, and we are continuing to provide it not at 7| per cent or 6f per cent but at 6J per cent. These are the figures which hon. members should keep in mind when they ask whether any thought has been given to the needs of the people in low income brackets.
I am sure that all hon. members regardless of party will agree that the figures I have just cited show that the effort of the federal government to assist the Canadian housing program is a really magnificent one. Possibly we could do more. We would if the money were readily available. But as the Minister of Finance pointed out a few moments ago there are two ways of raising money, by taxation or by borrowing. The federal government is lending money for housing in the rural areas at the rate of only 5 per cent. What reference has been made to that in this house during the last two days? We are continuing to lend this money at 5 per cent, yet this has not been mentioned. We are also continuing to lend it for university housing, and under the new legislation we shall make it available for college and technical and vocational school housing and the interest rate there is 6J- per cent, not 7,j- per cent. The same is true of other loans to municipalities for projects which have an important bearing on housing. Sewage treatment loans are continuing at the level of 6j per cent. Have we heard any reference to this action by the government in the last two days?
Would the minister permit a question? Will he tell us which administration started the loans for sewage projects?

Yes. If the hon. member had been following the debates on housing in the last year or so he would have heard me say on more than one occasion that these loans were started under the former government, and I gave due credit for that.

November 24, 1966
I should like very much to hear it again.

When my time is limited I do not like to repeat compliments that I have already paid.
I wish to assure the committee of the government's genuine interest in housing of all kinds, especially in housing for people with low incomes, the elderly and the others who need special assistance in this field.
We want action, not interest.

Well you are getting it. As was pointed out by my parliamentary secretary earlier this evening, there is a class of people with incomes of $10,000, $12,000, $15,000 or more who wish to build homes. Some are already occupying housing units, and they are buying expensive automobiles and expensive furniture and are paying for colour television sets at interest rates of between 9 and 11 per cent, or even higher. Why should these people not pay 7J per cent for housing and make more money available at lower interest rates for those in Canada who really need it and cannot afford it?
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
As I say, at this particular time we must attract a larger flow of private funds into the mortgage field, and after getting the advice of the Bank of Canada and of the Department of Finance and the experts who advise C.M.H.C. we are firmly convinced that this can only be done by allowing the N.H.A. interest rate to become reasonably competitive in the market and by providing flexibility so that the rate can change with changing market conditions.
This was pointed out by the hon. member for York North earlier today when he quoted from the report of the Porter commission, a commission set up by the previous government, a commission presided over by a distinguished jurist, the chief justice of Ontario, a man who had appreciable experience not only as provincial treasurer of Ontario but in municipal affairs and in the economic development of that province before becoming provincial treasurer. That report recommended almost exactly what was announced by the government on Tuesday night, a fluctuating interest rate. The Porter commission recommended an interest rate 1J, per cent above the interest rate being paid by the federal government on its long-range borrowings, and this is exactly the figure now in effect. Seven and a quarter per cent is 1J per cent above the cost of money, the interest that the
Supply-Finance
federal government pays on its long-range borrowings.
Little reference has been made in this committee to the fluctuating provision in the formula. The traditional lenders, the insurance companies, mortgage companies, banks and others, have more money today for investment than was available to them last year. Last year they were heavily committed at this time of the year because of the hundreds of millions of dollars worth of pulp and paper plants being constructed. This is a field in which I have at least a little knowledge. Those plants are completed or are now nearing completion. At least three of them have been brought into operation in British Columbia this year. Thus the need for money for office buildings, for other service units and for industrial expansion is now not so great, and our information is that these lending institutions will have more money available for lending in 1967 than they had this year.
If we really believe in a free enterprise economy, is it reasonable to suggest to these people that they should lend their money at per cent when the Porter commission and all the economists who have studied this problem have recommended that the spread should be 1J per cent over what the government pays? That is all that we are trying to do by this measure, and it will have a very desirable effect. It will bring in more money and will help correct the very serious housing situation that has developed within the last few months.
It is a matter of experience that a spread of 150 basis points between the National Housing Act interest yield and long-term government bonds is necessary to ensure a significant flow of institutional funds into mortgages. The records of C.M.H.C. over the last 20 years show that this to be a fact. A narrower spread has always resulted in a reduction in the flow of funds. This spread has been declining since early 1966, and there is now a difference of only 93 basis points, a drop of more than one-half per cent. At this level approved lenders are virtually non-operative under the N.H.A. and are likely to remain so as long as that condition persists. Under these circumstances, and with this fluctuating formula, the government has temporarily increased the interest rate to 7J per cent.
At the same time we have introduced a procedure for quarterly review from March next onward to ensure the required flexibility. In the opinion of the experts who advise us-and both the Minister of Finance and I

November 24, 1966
Supply-Finance
have questioned them at length-this should accomplish two things. In the first place, it should bring about a transfer of mortgage funds from conventional mortgage companies to new housing. There is no difficulty today in borrowing money from many mortgage companies through the traditional form of lending, but you will have to pay 8 per cent or higher. People who want to borrow money on a house today, if they are good credit risks, have no great difficulty getting money at 8 per cent, 8J per cent or 9 per cent. On the basis of history, which shows that there should be a spread of 1J per cent, many people who are borrowing money from the conventional lenders and paying rates of 8 per cent or more will be able to get money at 7,1 per cent under the National Housing Act provisions.
It has been suggested by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich that six months will elapse before we can expect improvement from the new interest rate. I would point out that it is in the month of December that the conventional lenders finalize their investment programs for 1967, which will start in January of that year, and we made the announcement at this time so that they will know they can get 7-J per cent at least until the end of March, and that there will be no change unless economic conditions warrant the fluctuation that I have mentioned of one-quarter per cent.
May I ask the minister a question at this point?

I should prefer to answer questions at the end because my time is limited.
We believe that these companies will be in a position to find more money for investment in the first quarter of next year because of notice of this change at this time, something they could not do if the announcement were made in January, which was the time we gave a somewhat similar notice last year.
Second, the increase in the N.H.A. interest rate should bring about an over-all and substantial increase in the volume of mortgage funds for housing in 1967. Many of the remarks made by the hon. member for Danforth were constructive and worthy of most serious consideration. I wish time permitted discussion of them in more detail, but I was particularly interested in his remarks about the appearance of the president of the Economic Council of Canada before the prices committee today. I was interested to know if the hon. member had the opportunity of cross-examining the president and asking him if he had

any objection to the increase in the rate from 6J per cent to 7J per cent. My information is that no such question was asked.
I would have asked it but the reason I did not was that I did not think it fair to inject him into the middle of the political controversy raging today.

I thought perhaps it was because his answer might have been that the Porter commission had recommended it and he would not quarrel with it.
I am not suggesting that the higher rate of 7;\ per cent will not work some hardship on some. As was pointed out earlier, it will mean an increase of approximately $4.50 per month on the repayment of the average N.H.A. loan. There is no question but that this will be a burden for some people. I am sure the hon. member for Macleod, who is an economist, will bear me out, however, that this will tend to diminish the demand from many potential home owners, but this will work both ways. It may work a hardship on a relatively small number but it will provide a benefit to those who are now paying 8 per cent or 9 per cent for their money. The point is that it is better to have lending institutions meeting a reduced demand for N.H.A. loans at 7J per cent than to supply virtually no funds whatever at 6 J per cent.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Let me tell you what has happened. Fourteen months ago lenders were lending money at 6J per cent and were glad to do so. Two years ago they were prepared to lend it at an even lower interest rate. The situation, however, is very different today. They tell me that they are prepared to lend at a reasonably increased rate and will come back into the field. Because of their interest they have provided the money, as they did in 1965, to finance the erection of 100,000 homes or more. In the last six weeks the number of loans has gone down to a trickle of between 400 and 500 a month. There is a great difference. Yet we have the assurance that there will be a substantial increase in lending if the rate is reasonably in tune with the times.
Let me add one more point about the interest rate. The legislation which just has been passed in respect of N.H.A. loans will bring about a significant reduction in interest charges which are paid on mortgage loans for less expensive housing. The other day I heard that a purchaser of an older house was asked to pay 14 per cent interest on a mortgage.
November 24, 1966

This information has been verified. It is outrageous. This new legislation certainly will help to correct that situation.
I have referred already to public housing, housing for senior citizens and others. I should like, however, to supplement what was said by one or two speakers earlier this evening about the effect this increase will have on people in the low income tax brackets. A lot of any size today in a city costs a minimum of $5,000 and in many instances as much as $8,000 or $9,000. You might be able to put up a tent on that lot and get by but you would not be able to do much more than that. If we can provide funds in an increasing amount for people who are at an income level where they can afford to build houses on these lots which cost $5,000, $6,000 or $9,000, we will be releasing existing housing for others who under the new policy can move in, improve and be able to own houses of their own. Those who live on farms will be able to get help through the other fields to which I have referred.
My time is nearly up, Mr. Chairman, but I should like to say that the government regards the increase in the N.H.A. rate as perhaps an unpleasant step but one which is an essential one in the serious measures which must be taken to bring about an increase in housebuilding activity in Canada. I would expect that much of the increase which takes place will be in rental housing. That is where the fall-off has been of late. This is where most people with incomes from $400 a month to $10,000 a year must find their homes. They will make their homes in apartments until they have very substantial incomes. We need more money for that type of housing and it has to come from the conventional lenders. If they will not lend it unless the interest rate is increased half of one per cent, then we have to give it to them. More and more in every part of Canada, particularly in view of the trend toward urbanization, much of the demand is for rental housing. This demand must be met more effectively and I believe one of the greatest contributing factors will be the increase in the interest rate to approved lenders which was announced on Tuesday night.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask one question? This is not in the form of a criticism. I am merely asking for information. If the fluctuation in the N.H.A. interest rate is geared to the cost of money to the government, then there is a possibility that the rate may go higher than 1\ per cent. The minister did not speak of this but he did mention the
Supply-Finance
fact it could go down. It could also go up. Is that right?
Yes. We are hopeful it will go down but it could go up.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with a matter which is not related to what has been discussed so far but which is within the ambit of the Department of Finance. I do so because this is the only opportunity I will have. Tomorrow at five thirty or six o'clock, when this committee is engaged in the dizzy intoxication of shuffling hundreds of millions of dollars into the jaws of the juggernaut government, we will have no opportunity to say yes or no to the respective votes with which we will be dealing.
With regard to vote 15 of the Department of Finance I must register my objection and say that if I had the opportunity I would vote against this item in the way in which it is now constituted. A few days ago in the public accounts committee it was indicated that vote 15, as it was constituted in the previous fiscal year, was properly passed by this house. That being the case, while it may not have been wise to do so it was done legally and the government had the right to exercise the power it gave. My objection is to the use of the words, "to supplement other votes". This permits the government, as was the case in respect of the passage of appropriation bill No. 8 which involved $55 million less such payments as had been made, to appropriate any part of this money to any other vote in the estimates. For example, if the Secretary of State saw fit she could, with the approval of the Treasury Board of course, take $6 million or $8 million of this money and use it to purchase works of art. This would be a perfectly legitimate purchase. Members of the government may say of course that they would not do that. They would lift their eyes and blissfully and innocently say, "We would not do that". I do not accept that. They would do it if it seemed appropriate. This is the nature of the beast.
I wish to take this opportunity to register my objection and say that if I had the opportunity I would vote against this item so that next year I would not be faced with the statement that I should have voted against it when the opportunity arose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I just wish to say that I believe there are only five or six minutes left and I would hope that when we reach the end of the period the estimates of the Department of Finance could be approved.

November 24, 1966
Supply-Finance
This is the fourth day now that they have been before the house. I realize that the hon. gentleman who has just spoken did not say that this is the first consideration we have had of these estimates. This is the fourth day. If there is an argument that there has not been sufficient time, I do not think it applies to the Department of Finance and I hope that our estimates will be approved at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I rise at this point to register the strongest possible objection to what I can only describe as a sloppy and careless exercise of administrative and legislative responsibility on the part of the government as exemplified in the Department of Finance at the present time with regard to the specific subject of the leigslation having to do with deposit insurance. These estimates may have been before the committee on four occasions; I do not know.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The fact is, however, that we have been pressing the minister for four weeks, even longer than that, to get this legislation before us. The committee on finance, trade and economic affairs is sitting and has been sitting for some time. It has had before it now for two weeks or more representatives of the Canadian Bankers Association. The examination of those witnesses is drawing to a close. I hold no brief for the banks of this country as such, but I do hold a brief for the borrowing and business communities, large and small, in Canada.
We have been discussing the banking legislation in so far as this matter is concerned in a complete vacuum. It is not as though the Bank Act revisions suddenly descended upon this government or the Minister of Finance. They have been before them for three years and for at least a year and a half this minister has had in mind the enactment of a deposit insurance scheme; yet we have not had that legislation introduced. It condemns the House of Commons and the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs to an exercise in futility to review the Bank Act legislation without this new important scheme before us.
We are very close to the time limit placed upon us for consideration of these estimates and I believe that on behalf of this house, the citizens of this country and the borrowers of this country, large and small, I should make this protest. I make it because this is a typical example of the ineptitude, sloppiness and carelessness of this government and I do not think it should be allowed to get away with it without some protest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I just say a word about the deposit insurance proposals that the government has under consideration? First of all, I should like to remind the hon. member for Kamloops that I have only been the Minister of Finance for 11 months, which is not quite as long as he suggested.
It seemed longer than a year and a half.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It seems to be longer than that to me as well.
What about us?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The banking legislation was not the only legislation I had to consider when I took office. In fact I do not think the time is being wasted by considering this legislation. We are now discussing it with the provinces in principle and I know from the reports I have received from my officials that these consultations will probably result in better legislation than if we had introduced it first and had our consultations afterwards.
Why did you not have your consultations six months ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps that might have been better, but the deposit insurance legislation was only decided upon six months ago. The hon. member will recall that my predecessor did not propose this legislation. This is one of the innovations I made after I became minister. The hon. member will also realize that this legislation is not the result of a recommendation of the Porter commission. The Porter commission did recommend that banking should somehow be defined, and I know my hon. friend thinks we should be able to do this. Perhaps we will do so in due course, but in the meantime it may be very useful to have deposit insurance. Moreover, as my hon. friend knows, I should like to get this brought forward quickly so it can be considered with the banking legislation as a whole. It is not our intention, of course, to proceed to enact it at this session.

Mr. Chairman, I will be very brief. I should like to ask the Minister of Labour, who is the housekeeper for housing legislation, how he reconciles his announcement made the night before last regarding the increase in interest rates, because money was not available and the interest rate did not attract lenders, with the answer he gave on October 21, 1966 to a question I asked him about the drying up of mortgage money in the Peterborough area. The answer he gave is
November 24, 1966	COMMONS
recorded at page 8954 of Hansard and it reads in part as follows:
I am very happy to be able to answer the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac. At that time I intimated that I did not think that all loans had been cut off in Peterborough and I find that to be correct. In recent weeks there has actually been a marked improvement in loans in that area and elsewhere.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I take great pleasure in presenting to the committee the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare for the year 1967. Because of the time problem I intend to be brief so that members will have as much time as possible for the consideration of these estimates.
At the outset I should mention that the main estimates were subjected to a detailed scrutiny by the standing committee on health and welfare during eight sittings last summer. This examination proved to be very helpful from my point of view and I hope to hon. members as well.
I might also point out that there is a resolution on the order paper relating to guaranteed income security for old age pensioners. I hope this will be before the house very soon, and this will afford an opportunity to discuss the whole subject of income maintenance for Canada's senior citizens.
Since the estimates of the minister's department were last considered by this committee the Canada Asssistance Plan legislation was adopted by parliament in mid-July. Subsequently steps have been taken to ensure its effective implementation. The provisions of the plan relating to mothers' allowances have been put into effect and all provinces have submitted claims respecting their mothers' allowance programs and have benefited in the amount of $18,900,000.
Intensive discussions have taken place with the provinces on the development of regulations required prior to the signing of agreements under Part I of the act. Officials of the department have visited all provinces at least once for discussions on regulations to ensure that the regulations will meet with the various conditions which are to be found across Canada.
The aim is to have the plan clearly reflect its objective as a broad and flexible public assistance measure. The regulations will be submitted to the provinces for review in the near future and agreements can then be entered into with the provinces. The target date for the signing of the agreements is January 1, 1967.

As all hon. members know, the Health Resources Fund Act was passed on June 27 of this year. The advisory committee as authorized by that act has been established and held its first meeting on October 6 and 7. At this meeting the preliminary five year programs which the acts requires provinces to prepare were reviewed and a number of urgent programs within them identified. Regulations respecting the time and manner of payment are now in the course of preparation and will be enacted shortly.
Mr. Chairman, I wish now to turn to the printed estimates and explain briefly the highlights. The estimates as originally tabled were in the amount of $1,263 billion, plus $1,035 billion for payments from the old age security fund. Subsequently supplementary estimates amounting to $2.1 million have been tabled. The supplementary estimates are mainly to cover the administration expenses of the proposed guaranteed minimum income program and an increase in family assistance payments to newly arrived immigrants.
I would like the committee to consider both the supplementary and main estimates at this time. These amount in the total to $2.3 billion, including the old age security fund, and are explained as follows: Old age security fund; it is estimated that payments from this fund will amount to $1,035 billion. Statutory items are estimated at $1,144 billion. Items to be voted by parliament amount to $121.1 million, made up of $119 million in the main estimates and $2,100,000 in the supplementary estimates.
The total increase over last year is $1,719,000. This is the result of an increase of $130 million in old age security payments, a decrease of $134,400,000 in budgeted statutory items and an increase of $6,100,000 in voted items.
The decrease of $134.4 million in budgeted statutory items relates mainly to the opting out by the province of Quebec from various cost-sharing programs in accordance with agreements reached under the Established Programs (Interim Arrangements) Act and to the reduction in the spendings on old age assistance, disabled persons allowances and blind persons allowances programs caused by the recent lowering of the old age security eligibility age to 69 and the scheduled reduction to 68 on January 1, 1967.
The main items making up the increase of $6.1 million in voted items are, a $2.8 million increase for salaries and wages, a major part of which is the transfer of 205 positions in

prosthetic services from the Department of Veterans Affairs, a $1.3 million increase for the administration of the proposed guaranteed minimum income program requested in supplementary estimates C, a $1 million increase for the operation of medical services mainly due to increases of native population and the opening of new facilities such as the Charles Camsell hospital, a $1.5 million increase in family assistance due to a forecast increase in the rate of immigration into Canada, of which $750,000 is requested in supplementary estimates A, a $900,000 increase in the grant to the University of British Columbia for the construction of a health science centre, a $800,000 increase in cash required to meet commitments to provinces under general health grants, and an increase of $500,000 in national welfare grants as approved for the fourth full year phase of the program. Offsetting these main increases is, of course, a decrease of almost $3.7 million in the provision for the construction of the Charles Camsell hospital. That briefly is the general picture of the department's spending program for the current year.

Leader of the Opposition. The allowance is $2,000 per hospital bed and $750 per bed for living quarters for nurses and interns. These amounts have not been increased.

There is nothing to indicate any increase to take care of the rising costs of the operation of hospitals. There was nothing in any previous legislation brought forward by the minister and there is certainly nothing in these estimates to indicate that this will be done. There was nothing in the speech we have just heard to indicate an increase in grants in this field. The minister knows, because I am sure

I assume, Mr. Chairman, that we are still on vote 1 and I wish to return to a question I asked of the minister in the house yesterday. I think it is terribly important that we arrive at a decision in this regard very quickly. I put my question on the order paper some months ago and the parliamentary secretary gave me an answer at the time regarding studies which are being made.
The problem in brief outline is that at the end of last week the Department of Health, Education and Welfare of the United States ordered that all 1968 automobiles sold in the United States in 1968 should be equipped with anti-fume devices because of the serious pollution threat in that country. I recognize that the problem in Canada is not entirely similar but there is an important body of opinion which says we are already polluting the air in our metropolitan areas such as the metropolitan regions of Toronto, Montreal and similar places.
I do not believe there is any need for further studies. I should like the minister to assure this committee that the same regulations as apply in the United States shall apply in Canada. There may be people ready to advise the minister along the following lines, that measurements have been taken in some of our large metropolitan areas and they show that no crisis has yet arisen. This is the same old story. All too often we wait for the crisis to arise and then we attempt to do something about it. If we act now we can save dollars and we can solve this problem before it becomes worse. While admittedly we do not yet face the same serious problem as that which faces Philadelphia, New York and Los Angeles county, we are nevertheless polluting the air in Canada in the same way as we are

DEBATES	November 24, 1966
polluting our waterways. The more time we waste, the more expensive it will be when we are finally obliged to confront the situation we have created.
I say to the minister: if all new cars sold in the United States in 1968 are to be fitted with anti-fume devices by federal law, can he not guarantee to this committee tonight that Canadian citizens will be protected by federal legislation just as United States citizens are to be protected by United States law and that the federal government in Canada intends to ordain that all new cars in 1968 will be equipped with anti-fume devices so that our own people can receive protection similar to that provided for citizens of the United States?
Let the minister not tell us there is need for further consideration. I have consulted with the motor industry and if they can fool the Canadian government they will do so. If we can be convinced, like good northern colonials, that we are not polluting the air, we shall not have this safety measure applied in Canada. I repeat: there is no need for further studies. Let us not wait until the air in our metropolitan areas has been polluted. Let us act now and get a head start on the problem. Let the minister guarantee that something will be done.

However, I can tell the minister that most of the time I have been in parliament most of my correspondence has been with respect to pensions of various kinds, and at the present time it is running higher than ever with respect to old age pensions.
Letter after letter comes day after day from individuals who, receiving the old age pension, have enjoyed the dignity and self-respect that goes with getting it without any test but who are concerned and feel a sense of humiliation and despondency over the fact that the day may soon come when, in order to get the full amount of the federal pension, they will have to submit to some kind of test or to report their income, and even the right of appeal in the proposed legislation does not get away from that.
I almost feel I should say to myself that it is stretching the rule to be talking about a piece of legislation that is going to be before us next week but I do it, Mr. Chairman, because I think this kind of plea ought to be made to the minister at this time. He has got several days in which to put both of these pieces of legislation in the form in which they ought to be, medicare and old age pensions, and I urge him to take full advantage of these few days. One of my colleagues suggests to me some good advice to pass on to the minister, that the Minister of Finance should be sent to Bermuda for the next three or four days so that the Minister of National Health and Welfare can make his own decision with respect to these important matters.
I hope the minister will tell us something about the situation with respect to grants to the provinces for the construction of hospitals. It seems to me the time has come either to raise the amount that the federal government contributes per hospital bed or to introduce some kind of percentage formula so that the needs for hospital construction across the country can be better met.
I would like to hear the minister reply to the point raised by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, both on orders of the day and this evening, and I shall content myself on this occasion by referring to just one other matter. I have in mind the many tragedies that take place because small children get

hold of bottles of lemon oil furniture polish and items of that kind, and in many instances actual death takes place. I have had some correspondence with the minister about this matter and, as he knows, my colleague from Hamilton South has a private members' bill on the order paper dealing with the subject.
The correspondence I have had with the minister raises the whole problem of federal-provincial jurisdiction, but surely this is a matter about which concern ought to lead to some action at an early date, whether it be legislation to prohibit the production of the kinds of substances that are lethal when small children get them or whether it be provision for better marking of the bottles and containers. On this point I hear my colleague from New Westminster urging me to say something about another poisonous product, but I do feel that poisonous substances in furniture polishes and other household items should be of concern to the minister.
My time is limited, Mr. Chairman, and there are others who wish to speak. I do not feel as badly as some may over the fact that we do not have a great deal of time to deal with these estimates in the house, simply because we did have a good go at them in committee. In conclusion, if the minister really wants a compliment from this source I tell him he has the opportunity to get it next week if he will bring in the medicare legislation to be effective when the government promised it, on July 1, 1967, and if he will bring in the old age pension increase without a means, needs or income test of any kind.
