subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the few moments allowed to me this evening to discuss the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare there are two points to which I should like to make reference. I support the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he states that in the committee on health and welfare we gave the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare a very thorough scrutiny. Certainly the minister produced all the officials whom any member of the committee might have wished to question. Their answers were frank; they were not answers which were censored and dictated by the minister as has been the case in respect of some other departments. We were given a great deal of information from the senior men, all of whom were experienced and knowledgeable in their own field of endeavour.
November 24, 1966	COMMONS DEBATES	10337
If hon. members would take the time to read the report of the committee on health and welfare they would find that we were asking serious questions of the senior men in the department as to whether or not overtime is paid to the employees and nursing staff of hospitals which are under federal control. In the estimates you will find numerous references to overtime in piddling amounts of $1,000, $2,000 and sometimes as high as $5,000. Inquiries as to what this overtime covered brought out the fact that the clerical staff sometimes is paid time and a half if called in to work on a Sunday or on a statutory holiday. The question concerning whether or not extra time is paid to the nursing staff elicited the information that the women who render such valuable service in this field of health care are paid straight time on a 40-hour week basis under the Department of National Health and Welfare. We were advised that under the Canada Labour Code if they were allowed to work overtime they could get time and a half in some cases but that in most cases they were forced to take time off.
I am a member of the health and welfare committee and when we were examining the estimates of the department I was privileged to go along with other members of the veterans affairs committee to Europe. I deliberately spent a day and a half checking with the authorities there in respect of the operation of their national health scheme. I subscribe to a British publication called "Nursing Mirror" which I find very interesting and forward looking. I not only spoke to senior officials in the British department of health, but also had an enjoyable hour and a half with the senior staff of the "Nursing Mirror". I was pleased to learn that in this field Britain is setting the pace. I do wish that we in Canada would follow their example of paying a premium rate of pay for Sundays to the nursing staff. All over the world there is a terrific shortage of nurses. This is something which has been mentioned by every speaker when speaking on the subject of national health services. I know we are on item 1 in these estimates but in vote 5 there is an item called "professional training grant to assist in an extended program for the training of health and hospital personnel".
In Canada, were it not for the married women who are fully trained nurses and are willing to register on the staffs of hospitals and were it not for the nurses we are able to bring in from the Philippines, Jamaica and Great Britain, who are willing to come to this
23033-654^
Supply-National Health and Welfare country and leave behind the country where they gained their training, we would not be able to keep our hospitals open. I maintain that if Canadian hospitals paid a premium rate of pay to nurses on Saturdays, Sundays and statutory holdays, over and above what is known as the regular five day week, we would be able to attract young women into the nursing profession. We have a serious shortage of nurses simply because the hours of work are not satisfactory and the remuneration is not large enough to attract young girls into spending their lives in a very necessary service. I think it is absolutely ridiculous that we have in Canada a shift differential for nurses only in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Quebec. In British Columbia shift differentials are paid to other than nurses in the hospitals. An interesting anomaly is that in British Columbia hospital personnel other than nurses are willing to accept shift differentials but the nurses are not, although they gladly accept them in Saskatchewan and Quebec.
If the federal government is willing to make a contribution toward the shift differentials paid to nurses in Quebec and in Saskatchewan, I wonder why the federal department of National Health and Welfare could not demand of the other provinces that shift differentials be paid throughout the length and breadth of Canada. Since we have shown we are willing to pay the cost of shift differentials in two provinces, and in the case of hospital personnel other than nurses in British Columbia, it must be apparent to the other provinces in the Dominion that they could introduce shift differentials in their hospital operations and secure federal support in that field if they would follow the example of Quebec and Saskatchewan in that regard. Could we not also follow the wonderful example of Great Britain where in the last two years they have been paying a day premium to those nurses who work on Sundays? At the present time in Britain they are only paying extra for Sunday work and they told me that for the past two years they have been paying one pound sterling extra for the nurses who report for duty on Sundays.
In Canada in the past when this has been discussed we have always been met by the' statement that surely you would not pay extra on Sunday and bring in nurses who would not. work on the other days of the week. They said that by doing this we would have difficulty in finding nurses who would work during the week days. The answer to this is provided by the experience in Great Britain. There are
10338	COMMONS
Supply-National Health and Welfare many, many nurses, particularly those who are married, who are quite prepared to nurse from Monday morning to Friday evening but who are not prepared to sacrifice their Saturdays and Sundays. If this premium pay were to be paid over the week end it would attract back to the hospitals other nurses who would be willing to work on the holidays because of the higher rate of pay for a shorter number of hours.
When I asked in Great Britain whether they found that the nurses on the floors of the hospitals demanded that they be given the opportunity to work on Sunday because of the extra pay, they laughed and said that far from that being the case the girls do not want to work on the week ends. They said that they work from Monday to Saturday noon and that 85 per cent of the staff is different on Sundays when they pay the extra bonus. There are registered nurses who will come out for the extra bonus on Sunday who will not work the other days of the week. I was advised that if it were not for the contribution of these people who have been attracted to the floors of the hospitals by the premium rate of pay the hospitals in Great Britain could not satisfactorily operate seven days a week on a 24-hour a day basis.
An interesting sidelight on this situation is the fact that when I asked these people in Great Britain if they were paying a premium rate of pay for a national holiday

that was the word I used-they said, "we call it a bank holiday." Call it what you like. In Canada we would call it a national holiday. If you wish to call it a bank holiday, that is all right. I said, "If you pay an extra pound on Easter Sunday, do you pay an extra pound on Easter Monday?" They said, "No, Mondays and Saturdays are part of the regular working week." I said, "How can you pay a woman an extra pound for working on Easter Sunday and not pay her extra for working on Easter Monday when the nation as a whole is on a holiday?" I was asked by the officials of the department of health in London not to speak so loudly because their expenses had gone up enough in respect of the Sundays without bringing the extra holidays into the act.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
However, I am certain that in Britain they will reach the day when they will voluntarily pay the extra pay on bank holidays and on Saturdays in order to attract back to the hospitals those people who do not wish to work as much as a five day week. I should like to see the day premium rate pay plan introduced

DEBATES	November 24, 1966
in Canadian hospitals, and I should like to see the federal government introduce this method of pay in hospitals under the jurisdiction of various departments, particularly the Department of Veterans Affairs.
The overtime and shift differential payments of the Department of Veterans Affairs are a disgrace. They amount to 8 cents an hour on evening shift and 12 cents an hour on night shift, but only apply between the hours of 6 p.m. and 6 a.m. My only comment on that situation is that it has taken years to get any shift differential in hospitals under the jurisdiction of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I have congratulated the Minister of Veterans Affairs on several occasions for having introduced this shift differential in veterans hospitals, but the Treasury Board introduced the most ridiculous hours of payment of which I have ever heard.
I referred to this situation in the committee discussions on the matter. Shift differential is only paid between 6 p.m. in the evening and 6 a.m. in the morning, so if a nurse is working from midnight to 8 a.m., on what everybody else would call the night shift, she gets twelve cents an hour from midnight to 6 a.m. and regular pay from 6 a.m. to 8 a.m. If she is working from 4 p.m. to midnight on the evening shift she gets the regular rate of pay from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. and the evening rate of differential from 6 p.m. to midnight. When you consider that such an individual would be receiving 8 cents an hour it must be obvious that she would pick up an extra 48 cents for working the evening shift compared with working the day shift. I wish the Department of National Health and Welfare would include a statement in its estimates to cover rate differentials as the Department of Veterans Affairs does in order that the hospitals under its jurisdiction could follow the example set by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Over and above that, I wish both departments, the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of National Health and Welfare, would pay day premium rates of pay and set an example for the whole of the Dominion of Canada. If we make the remuneration satisfactory to these young girls I am sure we will get a tremendous influx of young women in our schools of nursing, with the result that we will not have a shortage in that very vital element of our national life.
Time is running short and I wanted to speak at some length on a question involving malpractice insurance for hospitals in Canada. This is a deep subject and one that must
November 24, 1966	COMMONS DEBATES
receive the immediate attention of provincial and federal governments. There is a tremendous case going on right now in the courts involving one hospital in this country and a large sum of money.
Doctors demand that hospitals carry malpractice insurance coverage. I can tell you from personal experience that it is very difficult for hospitals to get satisfactory malpractice insurance coverage because insurance companies do not like to place this type of insurance. When an insurance company does give malpractice coverage many types of individuals are covered. The troubles connected with malpractice assurance are not confined specifically to the medical field. They relate to human nature. If malpractice insurance is carried by a hospital, a practitioner knowing that he is protected against any lawsuit for damages may well decide to let the insurance companies worry about a situation which may arise. These companies do not like to provide this kind of insurance and I for one do not blame them.
When an insurance company in this country does cover a hospital with malpractice insurance it includes a limiting clause in the policy which states that the insurance company can make its own settlement with any claimant and the hospital or doctor must agree to that settlement. One can see readily that there is something seriously wrong with this entire business. These insurance companies could not care less about making an admission that a doctor or a hospital was at fault if they can settle for $1,500 or $2,000, because they may save themselves a great deal of money by settling out of court. The insurance company will readily blacken the name of the hospital or the doctor if they can prevent a claimant from taking a case to court, as a result of wh ch they may have to pay $10,000, $20,000 or $30,000.
The three companies in Canada that issue malpractice insurance for hospitals all have limiting clauses in their policies to the effect that they can make a settlement with the claimant and if the insured, being the hospital or the doctor, refuses to accept the settlement the insurance company does not have to pay any sum over and above that original proposed settlement which may be awarded by a court of law. This is a ridiculous situation because no coverage whatsoever is given under the guise of malpractice insurance. I maintain and believe that even at my age I will live to see the day when the hospitals of the various provinces have co-operative insurance in respect of malpractice. This type of
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion insurance as in effect in the state of California at the present time where there used to be a large number of lawsuits against hospitals and doctors.
In Canada doctors are protected by the Canadian Medical Protective Association which has its head office here in Ottawa. It is practically compulsory to have a co-operative effort in respect of malpractice insurance and doctors have found this highly valuable. I maintain that hospitals will follow the example set in California and adopt a scheme of co-operative malpractice insurance and get away from this so-called coverage by private carriers of insurance who have limitations in their contracts. These policies do not adequately cover this field to the satisfaction of the hospitals and doctors of this nation.
This is a very vital fact in the practice of medicine and the provision of hospital services in this country, and I sincerely urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare to take the lead in establishing co-operative malpractice insurance in the hospitals in the provinces which make up the Dominion of Canada, along the lines now in effect in the state of California. In this way every doctor and hospital would be fully covered, and the hospitals and doctors would not have to rely on insurance companies which are willing to admit malfeasance, so to speak, in order to settle on a small scale rather than protect the reputation and name of an individual hospital or doctor for fear of facing a larger settlement.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.

subsubtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REGULATIONS RESPECTING BONUS TO BILINGUAL EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I have to say tonight I could say in my own riding to a receptive and agreeable audience, no doubt, but what good would that do? I might better say it here even though some hon. members may disagree. I rise this evening pursuant to my question in the house on Friday last. At that time I asked the following question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson):
Mr. Speaker, will the new bonus to be paid bilingual civil servants also be paid to civil servants
10340	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion who are bilingual in any language combination other than English and French?
Since then I have had the opportunity to point out to the house the shallow, supine and discriminatory policy being practised by the government in this regard, because they do not intend to give recognition to any bilingual civil servants other than those they wish to placate, namely, those of French origin who can speak some English. I pointed out to the house that there are people of other racial origins all across Canada working for the government who are bilingual in other languages. But, of course, it is evident that these people are regarded by the Pearson government as second-class citizens. I say to the Prime Minister-this is my main reason for rising in my place tonight-and I say it on behalf of millions of Canadians, that he and his government have gone far enough with the bilingual and bicultural patronage system that he has so foolishly adopted. He has gone far enough with this devilish plan that day by day is dividing Canada.
We all have our linguistic rights in this country. No language is outlawed. In fact, they are all indispensable to those who use their particular language. None of them is second class. But now, mainly due to the patronizing attitude of this government toward what seems to be a fanatical racist and linguistic demand, I am informed that there are members of this house who will not accept a messenger summoned to a member's office if that messenger does not speak French. I will accept any messenger who can perform the duties I ask of him, regardless of his mother tongue. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I like to have a French messenger so that I can speak French to him and learn more of that noble language. If there are members of this house who think I am speaking just to hear myself talk, I say without any doubt in my mind that no English speaking member of the house has ever sent a messenger from his office because of his mother tongue.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I would remind hon. members who may think I am speaking just to hear myself talk that 67 per cent of Canadians speak English only, 19 per cent of Canadians speak French only, 13 per cent are bilingual and 1 per cent speak other tongues only. These figures are reliable because they were taken from the last census.
The hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac <Mr. Webb) and the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) both raised the question of the wholesale discharge of the last 18 English

DEBATES	November 24, 1966
speaking government telephone operators on Parliament Hill. They received no satisfaction in reply to their questions. There are 60 operators in total. The discriminatory policy of this Pearson government could not even allow these last 18 employees to remain even though they were less than one-third of the total. They had to go only because they were English speaking, because they were no doubt Anglo-Saxon. This government makes it clear that it is very much out of caste, context and custom to be of Anglo-Saxon race or extraction these days. I resent this.
There is a row on in the Liberal caucus, they tell me, and I give great credit to those Liberal members who are resisting government policy in this respect. I note that this evening's edition of the Ottawa Citizen quotes the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Tucker) on this question as follows:
The need for bilingual civil servants is grossly exaggerated.
How correct is the hon. member for Trinity-Conception. In the same article he called the replacement of the English speaking operators "discrimination of the worst kind".
A society works, Mr. Speaker, mainly because its institutions and regulations are accepted to be the way of life for the majority. But in order to achieve the fullest measure of success a culture must accept and allow for a tolerable range of temperamental differences of its citizens, not just for the average or the mean. It is a give and take arrangement that is mutually rewarding.
If I may refer once more to the bilingual clerks who will receive the 7 per cent government largesse under this measure, we have the clerk who cannot qualify, probably because he speaks English and perhaps another language other than French, working alongside the clerk who does qualify under this narrow, discriminatory measure, but the former has to pay taxes to contribute to the 7 per cent bonus enjoyed by his office mate. In other words, this government makes part of the civil service pay a special salary to a chosen few. This is one of the death throes of the Pearson-sponsored bilingualism and bicul-turalism; this particular aspect has gone completely awry.
Bilingualism, Mr. Speaker, is a good thing if it does not exclude languages other than French. There are many people in our civil service who can speak more than two languages. This government would discriminate against them. Those qualities and attributes of
November 24, 1966
a linguistic cosmopolite this government does not recognize. The attributes that make for better relationships with our many neighbours in the world this government does not recognize. All they think about is a few votes in certain parts of the country that will perpetuate their poisonous form of politics and placate a few people.
The Liberal party embraced bilingualism here in the capital and we agreed with it to a certain limited extent, but the Liberal party does the opposite in the province of Quebec. They reject bilingualism and embrace and adopt unilingualism. I have reference here to a recent article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen reporting on the latest provincial Liberal party meeting in Quebec. The Ottawa Citizen is not unfavourable to the Liberal party and on November 21 it carried an article headed "Bilingualism Row: Issue Sparks Uproar Among Quebec Grits". The issue involved was bilingualism. They have no use for it down there. This is typical of the Liberal party and always has been. There are no truths in Liberalism, only deception.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say at the outset that the type of attack launched in this house by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox is totally unwarranted.
On behalf of the President of the Treasury Board I have the following statement to make in reply to the hon. member. On the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission the Treasury Board has established, by Treasury Board Minute 658237 of October 20, 1966, a differential of 7 per cent of the actual rate of pay, rounded to the nearest dollar, received by employees in secretarial, stenographic and typing positions in which adequate performance of duties and effective service to the public requires the use of both official languages, and has approved payment of the differential to incumbents of such positions who are required to use and are actually using a second official language at least 10 per
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion cent of their time in the performance of their duties and are qualified by the Civil Service Commission as meeting an appropriate standard of competence in the two official languages.
The Treasury Board minute requires the deputy head to certify that an employee is qualified by the Civil Service Commission as meeting an appropriate standard of competence in the two official languages, and provides that payment of the differential may be made with effect from a date not earlier than October 1, 1966, provided the deputy head applies to the Civil Service Commission for a test of competence and the employee is qualified by the commission before February 1, 1967.
Employees occupying positions in the secretarial, stenographic and typing group may be deemed to have been qualified by the Civil Service Commission as meeting an appropriate standard of competence in the two official languages if, at the time of their appointment, the essential qualifications included knowledge of both official languages under the provisions of section 47 of the Civil Service Act. Other employees in such positions must submit to a test of competence in the other official language in order to qualify for the differential.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
In future, any candidate for appointment in this group claiming competence in both official languages or any employee already in the group who believes that he has acquired the necessary proficiency may be tested in both languages for the purposes of meeting this particular condition for payment of the language differential. In these cases the differential would be payable with effect from the date of the appointment if the other conditions are met.
In instances in which an employee who was not tested on appointment and who was found, after February 1, 1967, to occupy a position for which the differential was warranted, the differential will be payable with effect from the date on which the commission is requested to establish the competence of the employee concerned.
